Semi-Dirac spin liquids and frustrated quantum magnetism on the trellis lattice

August 24, 2026
Abstract

Geometrical frustration in quantum magnets provides a fertile setting for unconventional phases of matter, including quantum spin liquids (QSLs). The trellis lattice, with its complex site arrangements and edge-sharing triangular motifs, presents a promising platform for such physics. In this work, we undertake a comprehensive classification of all fully symmetric QSLs on the trellis lattice using the projective symmetry group approach within the Abrikosov-fermion representation. We find 7 U(1) and 25 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} short-ranged Ansätze and analyze the phase diagram in the mean-field parameter space, uncovering both gapped and Dirac QSLs as well as a semi-Dirac spin liquid that emerges at the level of projective symmetry group classification and mean-field band structure, in which the spinon dispersion is linear along one momentum direction but quadratic along the orthogonal one. We demonstrate that such dispersions can occur only at high-symmetry points in the Brillouin zone with C2​vC_{2v} little groups and analyze their characteristic correlation signatures. Moreover, by optimizing over all symmetry-allowed mean-field states, we map out a phase diagram—featuring six distinct phases—of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg Hamiltonian on the trellis lattice. Among these, we find four quasi-one-dimensional QSL phases, one dimer phase, and one Dirac QSL phase. Going beyond mean field, we also assess equal-time and dynamical spin structure factors of these phases using density-matrix renormalization group and Keldysh pseudofermion functional renormalization group calculations and compare qualitative momentum-space features of these spectra with those obtained at the mean-field level. Finally, we identify four cuprate and vanadate compounds as promising experimental realizations and provide spectroscopic predictions, based on first-principles Hamiltonians, as a guide for future neutron-scattering studies on these materials.

I Introduction

The investigation of magnetic properties of quantum materials has long been a central focus in condensed matter physics, particularly the intricate relationship between lattice topology and quantum orders [1, 2]. A key aspect of this interplay arises when specific geometric arrangements of magnetic moments give rise to competing interactions—an effect known as geometric frustration. Lattices containing triangular motifs serve as paradigmatic examples of such frustration, often exhibiting complex magnetic behavior such as spin-spiral states, non-coplanar orders, and, in certain cases, extensive ground-state degeneracy that suppresses conventional long-range magnetic order [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11].

Generically, quantum fluctuations at low temperature tend to destabilize classical magnetic order, pushing the system into a quantum paramagnetic regime. When such fluctuations are sufficiently strong—as alluded to above—they can lead to exotic phases of matter known as quantum spin liquids (QSLs), characterized by the absence of any spontaneous symmetry breaking even at zero temperature [12, 13, 14]. In recent years, the study of frustrated magnets has garnered significant attention, fueled by both theoretical and experimental evidence for QSL behavior in various two- and three-dimensional lattice geometries, including kagome, triangular, and pyrochlore structures [15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21].

Two-dimensional (2D) Heisenberg antiferromagnets on Archimedean lattices provide a rich platform for exploring the influence of lattice geometry and quantum fluctuations on magnetic phases [22, 23, 24, 25]. Of the eleven Archimedean lattices, four—namely the square [26, 27, 28], honeycomb [29, 30], square-octagon, and square-hexagon-dodecagon lattices—are unfrustrated and, as expected, support long-range magnetic order for the Heisenberg model with only nearest-neighbor interactions. The remaining seven incorporate geometrical frustration due to their corner- or edge-sharing triangular motifs. Among these, considering again nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic couplings of equal strength, the Shastry-Sutherland [31] and triangular [32, 33, 34] lattices maintain long-range order despite strong frustration, whereas the kagome and star lattices host magnetically disordered ground states. The remaining three lattices—maple leaf, trellis, and bounce—lie in an intermediate regime. In this list of candidates, the maple-leaf lattice, in particular, has been intensely studied in recent years [35, 36, 37, 38], revealing a variety of exotic phases, including an exact dimerized ground state [39] and possible quantum spin liquid behavior [40, 41, 42, 43].

In contrast, the trellis lattice has remained largely unexplored [44], despite its complex site arrangements and edge-sharing triangular connectivity that can host unconventional magnetic structures not typically found in simpler geometries. An early study employing various numerical and analytical techniques revealed a range of diverse magnetic and nonmagnetic phases on the trellis lattice [45]. It identified a nondegenerate valence-bond solid state in the dimer limit and a subextensively degenerate (gapless) Majumdar-Ghosh-like phase in the regime of weakly coupled zigzag chains, both of which have a finite singlet-triplet gap. Between these two extremes, gapless magnetically ordered phases emerge. Specifically, antiferromagnetic order appears near the honeycomb-lattice limit, while a helical state with incommensurate spin correlations develops along the chains when all three magnetic interactions compete. Extensions of this framework to include ferromagnetic couplings have also been explored [46, 47, 48]. The aforementioned gapped rung-dimer phase of the trellis lattice has been extensively investigated using perturbative methods and quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations [49, 50, 51, 52]. In particular, the dynamical structure factor (DSF)—interpreted in terms of triplon excitations—was computed in Ref. 53. Additionally, several works have examined coupled zigzag chains, which form the trellis lattice backbone, using methods such as the coupled-cluster approach [54] and the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) combined with linearized spin-wave analysis [55]. Notably, the trellis lattice can be regarded as a special case of a spatially anisotropic triangular lattice [56]. When third-nearest-neighbor couplings are set to zero on certain triangles of this anisotropic lattice, the system reduces to a trellis lattice antiferromagnet that supports a stripe like phase composed of alternately stacked one-dimensional (1D) spiral spin chains. These investigations already highlight the rich variety of ground states and excitation spectra that arise from the interplay between frustration, dimensional crossover, and quantum fluctuations in trellis lattice antiferromagnets. Even more interestingly, at the isotropic point, the ground state could be a quantum paramagnet [25], and possibly, a quantum spin liquid.

On the experimental front, the trellis lattice garnered significant attention following the synthesis of the layered cuprate compound SrCu2​O3\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} [57], in which magnetic Cu2+ ions form spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg ladders weakly coupled via frustrated interladder exchanges. Strong antiferromagnetic interactions favor singlet formation on the rungs of the ladders, resulting in a spin gap in the excitation spectrum [49]. Under appropriate doping or applied pressure, related cuprate ladder systems, such as Sr14-xCaxCu24O41, also exhibit superconductivity, suggesting an intrinsic tendency toward pair formation in these quasi-one-dimensional systems [58]. Subsequent studies extended trellis-lattice physics to layered vanadate compounds such as CaV2​O5\text{CaV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}} [59], MgV2​O5\text{MgV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}} [60], and Pb0.55Cd0.45V2O5 [61]. In these materials, V4+ ions form spin-1/21/2 planes with a trellis lattice geometry. Unlike in the cuprates, the interladder couplings in vanadates can be appreciable, as revealed by ab initio calculations [62, 63], magnetic susceptibility measurements [50], and Raman spectroscopy [64, 65]. More recently, quasi-one-dimensional organic magnets such as α\alpha-2-Cl-4-F-V [66] and β\beta-2,3,5-Cl3-V [67] have been synthesized. These molecular crystals, built from verdazyl radicals carrying spin-1/21/2, offer a platform for investigating quantum magnetism in low dimensions.

Despite these advances, our understanding of nonmagnetic phases on the trellis lattice remains limited. An important open question is whether the combined effects of geometrical frustration, quantum fluctuations, and lattice topology can stabilize exotic phases on this geometry, in particular, a quantum spin liquid at and around the isotropic point. Motivated by these considerations, our present work is devoted to a comprehensive investigation of the properties of various potential QSL ground states on the trellis lattice. Owing to their paramagnetic nature, QSLs cannot be described using the conventional Landau theory of spontaneous symmetry breaking. Instead, their classification involves internal symmetry structures governed by emergent SU(2) gauge degrees of freedom coupled to matter fields [68]. The projective symmetry group (PSG) framework [69, 70, 71] provides a powerful approach for the systematic identification and classification of distinct QSL phases by exploiting these emergent gauge structures. This formalism has been successfully employed for many 2D Archimedean lattices, including the square [69, 72], triangular [73, 74, 75], honeycomb [76, 77], kagome [78, 79, 80], star [81, 82], square-octagon [83], Shastry-Sutherland [84, 85], maple-leaf [43], and bounce [86, 87] lattices.

I.1 Outline of the manuscript

This paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we provide a brief introduction to the fermionic representation of spin-1/21/2 operators and outline the fundamentals of the PSG construction. Section III presents a detailed analysis of the full symmetry group of the trellis lattice, along with its projective extensions, defined up to elements of the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge groups. Focusing on the three symmetry-inequivalent nearest-neighbor bonds, we classify all distinct mean-field states corresponding to different QSLs that arise from the projective extensions of the full symmetry group. These states, along with their associated gauge structures and flux patterns, are summarized in Sec. IV. In Sec. V, we investigate the phases that emerge as the hopping parameters are varied within the mean-field description. We also construct a phase diagram in Sec. V.3 based on a spin-1/21/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, with exchange couplings JvJ_{v}, JzJ_{z}, and JhJ_{h} defined on the three symmetry-inequivalent nearest-neighbor bonds of the trellis lattice. The spectral properties of the various QSL states are then analyzed in Sec. VI, where we compute both the dynamical and equal-time structure factors (EQSFs) from our mean-field Ansätze as well as using state-of-the-art Keldysh pseudofermion functional renormalization group (pf-FRG) and DMRG calculations. Thereafter, Sec. VII provides an in-depth discussion on candidate compounds that realize the trellis lattice, using density functional theory (DFT) and Keldysh pf-FRG, thus outlining a pathway for the observation of this physics in future experiments on quantum materials. Finally, we conclude with a brief discussion of our results and their implications in Sec. VIII.

I.2 Summary of main results

As mentioned above, in this work, we implement the PSG construction within the Abrikosov-fermion (parton) representation of spin-1/21/2 operators to classify all distinct fully symmetric QSL states at the mean-field level that can be realized on the trellis lattice. Subsequently, we analyze the corresponding fermionic band structures and map out the associated phase diagram. Besides fully gapped and Dirac QSLs, we discover an intriguing semi-Dirac spin liquid state [88, 89, 90, 91, 92, 93, 94, 95, 96, 97, 98, 99, 100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105], for which the spinon dispersion is observed to be linear along one momentum direction but quadratic in the direction orthogonal to it.

For itinerant electrons, semi-Dirac dispersions have recently attracted considerable attention, as they arise from the merging of multiple Dirac points into a single one [89]. Semi-Dirac fermions naturally display strongly anisotropic characteristics: Along one direction the dispersion is quadratic, reflecting Galilean invariance, while along the orthogonal direction it remains linear, reflecting Lorentz invariance. A direct consequence of this anisotropy is the unconventional Landau-level scaling of B2/3B^{2/3} with a magnetic field BB, which has recently been reported in magneto-optical spectroscopy of ZrSiS and microscopically linked to nodal-line crossings in the material [88]. Thermal or charge transport, being inherently direction sensitive, offers an additional potential probe of semi-Dirac points. However, such measurements require a spectrally isolated semi-Dirac point to achieve a satisfactory signal-to-noise ratio. Despite their charge neutrality, many features of itinerant electrons can carry over to elementary spinon excitations in spin liquids, including their response to external magnetic fields [106]. In particular, thermal conductivity may serve as a probe of transport signatures from low-lying spinon excitations, although such measurements remain experimentally challenging [107, 108, 109].

Here, we demonstrate that semi-Dirac spinon dispersions can occur only at high-symmetry points in the Brillouin zone where the little group is C2​vC_{2v}, i.e., characterized by a twofold rotation symmetry and two orthogonal reflection symmetries. In contrast, momentum points in the Brillouin zone with larger little groups cannot host semi-Dirac dispersions. Scaling analysis further reveals that the equal-time spin-spin correlations in real space decay algebraically as ∼1/r3\sim 1/r^{3} and ∼1/r6\sim 1/r^{6} along the two orthogonal directions. Finally, we present both dynamical and equal-time spin structure factors, at the mean-field level, for semi-Dirac spin liquids (s-DSLs).

Within a self-consistent mean-field framework, we map out the quantum phase diagram of the most general nearest-neighbor Heisenberg antiferromagnetic Hamiltonian. This procedure entails optimizing over all symmetry-allowed U(1) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} mean-field Ansätze in order to identify the energetically favored solutions. Our analysis reveals six distinct phases, characterized by correlation patterns indicative of (I) zigzag-chain, (II) zigzag-ladder, (III) rung-chain, (IV) rung-ladder, (V) ladder-dimer, and (VI) honeycomb structures. For representative points within these phases, we further assess the role of gauge fluctuations beyond mean-field: at zero temperature using DMRG, and at finite temperature via Keldysh pf-FRG. These calculations reveal significant redistribution of spectral weight in particular within the ladder-dimer and honeycomb phases.

Furthermore, we identify four candidate materials—two cuprates and two vanadates—that can be modeled to good accuracy as two-dimensional systems with dominant Heisenberg interactions along the ladder (JvJ_{v}), rung (JhJ_{h}), and zigzag (JzJ_{z}) bonds. Using DFT combined with an energy-mapping approach, we extract the effective model parameters for CaCu2O3, SrCu2O3, MgV2O5, and CaV2O5. In these compounds, the Cu2+ and V4+ magnetic ions host S=1/2S=1/2 moments forming the underlying magnetic lattice, which takes the form of a flat trellis lattice in SrCu2O3 and a buckled trellis lattice in the other three compounds. The hierarchy of couplings places CaCu2O3 in close proximity to a one-dimensional limit, while SrCu2O3 and CaV2O5 reduce to coupled two-leg ladder systems, with the latter exhibiting substantially stronger rung couplings. In contrast, MgV2O5 displays comparable rung and chain couplings. These effective Hamiltonians are then analyzed using Keldysh pf-FRG, enabling the computation of dynamical spin structure factors at finite temperature. For CaCu2O3, we find excellent agreement between our calculated spectral functions and previously reported neutron scattering data, thereby validating our effective Hamiltonian. For SrCu2O3 and CaV2O5, the dynamical and equal-time structure factors closely resemble those expected for the rung-ladder and ladder-dimer phases, respectively, while MgV2O5 shows clear signatures of magnetic ordering. Our predictions for the dynamical structure factors of SrCu2O3 and CaV2O5 provide concrete benchmarks for future inelastic neutron scattering experiments.

II Theoretical framework

In this section, we outline the generic theoretical framework employed to investigate quantum spin liquid phases. We begin with the Heisenberg Hamiltonian,

ℋ^=∑⟨i​j⟩Ji​j​𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j,\hat{\mathcal{H}}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}J_{ij}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}, (1)

where 𝐒^i\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i} denotes the spin operator at site ii and Ji​jJ_{ij} represents the exchange coupling between sites ii and jj.

To capture the fractionalized nature of excitations characteristic of QSLs, we introduce charge-neutral, spin-1/21/2 quasiparticles known as spinons or partons. These quasiparticles can obey either bosonic or fermionic statistics. In this work, we adopt the fermionic representation, which conveniently allows for a unified treatment of both gapped and gapless QSLs. In the Abrikosov fermion formalism, the spin operators are expressed as [110, 111]

S^iα=12​∑σ​σ′f^i​σ†​τσ​σ′α​f^i​σ′,\hat{S}_{i}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}\tau^{\alpha}_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\sigma^{\prime}}, (2)

where α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z, σ,σ′∈{↑,↓}\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}, and τα\tau^{\alpha} are the usual Pauli matrices.

While this representation captures the essence of fractionalization, it enlarges the local Hilbert space. The physical spin Hilbert space at each site has dimension 2, corresponding to spin-up and spin-down states. However, in the fermionic representation, the local Hilbert space includes four states: two singly occupied (physical), and one each of doubly occupied and empty (unphysical). To project back to the physical Hilbert space, we impose the following local constraints:

∑σf^i​σ†​f^i​σ=1,∑σ,σ′f^i​σ​f^i​σ′​εσ​σ′=0,\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\sigma}=1,\quad\sum_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\sigma}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\sigma^{\prime}}\varepsilon^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}=0, (3)

where εσ​σ′\varepsilon_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}} is the rank-2 antisymmetric tensor.

The fermionic parton construction naturally gives rise to an emergent SU(2) gauge symmetry. This becomes explicit by introducing the SU(2) doublet field

ψ^i=[f^i↑f^i↓†f^i↓−f^i↑†],\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\uparrow}&\phantom{-}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}\\ \hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\downarrow}&-\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}\end{bmatrix}, (4)

in terms of which the spin operators can be compactly written as

S^iα=12​Tr​[ψ^i†​τα​ψ^i].\hat{S}_{i}^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}\left[\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}\tau^{\alpha}\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\right]. (5)

This representation reveals the invariance of spin operators under local SU(2) gauge transformations ψ^i→ψ^i​Wi\hat{\psi}_{i}\rightarrow\hat{\psi}_{i}W_{i}, with Wi∈SU⁡(2)W_{i}\in\mathrm{SU}(2).

Substituting Eq. (2) into the Heisenberg Hamiltonian (1) results in a quartic fermionic interaction term. To obtain a solvable theory, we perform a mean-field decoupling in the spin-singlet channel, which is appropriate for describing spin-rotation-invariant states. The relevant mean-field parameters are the singlet hopping, χi​j\chi_{ij}, and singlet pairing, Δi​j\Delta_{ij}, fields, defined as

χi​j\displaystyle\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij} =⟨∑σf^i​σ†​f^j​σ⟩,\displaystyle=\left\langle\sum_{\sigma}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j\sigma}\right\rangle, (6)
Δi​j†\displaystyle\Delta_{ij}^{\dagger} =−⟨∑σ,σ′f^i​σ​f^j​σ′​εσ​σ′⟩.\displaystyle=-\left\langle\sum_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i\sigma}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j\sigma^{\prime}}\varepsilon^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\right\rangle. (7)

The resulting mean-field Hamiltonian takes the form

H^MF\displaystyle\hat{H}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{MF}} =38∑i,jJi​j[12Tr(ui​j†ui​j)−Tr(ψ^iui​jψ^j†+h.c.)]\displaystyle=\frac{3}{8}\sum_{i,j}J^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\left[\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(u^{\dagger}_{ij}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij})-\mathrm{Tr}\left(\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{j}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)\right]
+∑i,μaμ(i)Tr[ψ^iτμψ^i†],\displaystyle+\sum_{i,\mu}a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mu}(i)\,\mathrm{Tr}\left[\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\tau^{\mu}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{i}\right], (8)

where ui​ju_{ij} is the SU(2) matrix-valued link field associated with the bond ⟨i​j⟩\langle ij\rangle, given by

ui​j=[χi​j†Δi​jΔi​j†−χi​j].u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}=\begin{bmatrix}\chi^{\dagger}_{ij}&\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\\ \Delta^{\dagger}_{ij}&-\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\end{bmatrix}. (9)

The last term in Eq. (8) imposes the single-occupancy constraint (3) at the mean-field level using Lagrange multipliers aμ​(i)a_{\mu}(i) for μ=1,2,3\mu=1,2,3. Together, the combination {ui​j,aμ​(i)}\{u_{ij},a_{\mu}(i)\} defines a mean-field Ansatz characterizing a quantum paramagnetic state.

Now, it is straightforward to verify that the mean-field Hamiltonian in Eq. (8) is invariant under local SU(2) gauge transformations of the form

ψ^i→ψ^i​Wi,ui​j→Wi†​ui​j​Wj,aα​τα→aα​Wi†​τα​Wi,\displaystyle\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\rightarrow\hat{\psi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i},\quad u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\rightarrow W_{i}^{\dagger}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j},\quad a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha}\tau^{\alpha}\rightarrow a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha}W_{i}^{\dagger}\tau^{\alpha}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}, (10)

where Wi∈SU⁡(2)W_{i}\in\mathrm{SU}(2) is a local gauge transformation matrix.

The physical implication of this gauge redundancy is that a given mean-field Ansatz {ui​j,aα}\{u_{ij},a_{\alpha}\} and its gauge-transformed counterpart {ui​j′,aα′}\{u^{\prime}_{ij},a^{\prime}_{\alpha}\} describe the same physical spin liquid state. In other words, different Ansätze related by local SU(2) gauge transformations are physically equivalent, whereas those not connected by such transformations correspond to distinct quantum paramagnetic phases. This redundancy can be exploited to classify and characterize QSL phases using projective symmetry considerations, as we elaborate on next.

An important consequence of the SU(2) gauge structure is that global and lattice symmetries may act on the fermionic operators in a projective manner. To illustrate this, consider a symmetry operation 𝒪\mathcal{O} from the lattice space group. Its naive action on the mean-field variables is to map ui​j→u𝒪⁡(i)​𝒪​(j)u_{ij}\rightarrow u_{\mathcal{O}(i)\mathcal{O}(j)}. If it happens that ui​j≠u𝒪⁡(i)​𝒪​(j)u_{ij}\neq u_{\mathcal{O}(i)\mathcal{O}(j)}, one might incorrectly conclude that the Ansatz breaks the symmetry 𝒪\mathcal{O}. However, the symmetry can still be preserved projectively if there exists a local SU(2) gauge transformation W𝒪​(i)W_{\mathcal{O}}(i) associated with 𝒪\mathcal{O} such that

W𝒪†​(𝒪⁡(i))​u𝒪⁡(i)​𝒪​(j)​W𝒪​(𝒪⁡(j))=ui​j.W_{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}(\mathcal{O}(i))\,u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}(i)\mathcal{O}(j)}\,W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}(\mathcal{O}(j))=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}. (11)

In this case, the combined operation of the lattice symmetry 𝒪\mathcal{O} and the corresponding gauge transformation W𝒪W_{\mathcal{O}} leaves the Ansatz invariant. The full set of such symmetry-gauge combinations {𝒪,W𝒪}\{\mathcal{O},W_{\mathcal{O}}\} defines the PSG. The PSG provides a classification scheme for QSLs, playing a role analogous to that of symmetry groups in the Landau paradigm of symmetry-breaking phases.

Within the PSG framework, one can also define an analog of the identity operation. Specifically, we define the invariant gauge group (IGG) as the subgroup of SU(2) gauge transformations 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} that leave the mean-field Ansatz invariant:

𝒢i†​ui​j​𝒢j=ui​j,𝒢i∈SU⁡(2).\mathcal{G}_{i}^{\dagger}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}\mathcal{G}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij},\qquad\mathcal{G}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\in\mathrm{SU}(2). (12)

The IGG thus characterizes the residual gauge freedom of the Ansatz and corresponds to the projective realization of the identity element in the symmetry group.

Although the IGG describes, in general, a local symmetry operation, one can always choose a gauge such that the IGG only involves global elements of either SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) or its subgroups, U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), or ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}. For such a gauge choice, the Ansatz is said to be in its canonical form, and its IGG structure becomes manifest. To make this explicit, we parametrize the SU(2) link variable ui​ju_{ij} in terms of four real numbers λi​jμ\lambda^{\mu}_{ij} as

ui​j=i​λi​j0​τ0+∑μ=13λi​jμ​τμ.u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}=i\lambda^{0}_{ij}\tau^{0}+\sum_{\mu=1}^{3}\lambda^{\mu}_{ij}\tau^{\mu}. (13)

Based on this parametrization, different IGG structures emerge:

  1. (a)

    If λi​jμ=0\lambda^{\mu}_{ij}=0 for μ=1,2,3\mu=1,2,3, then the IGG is global SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2).

  2. (b)

    If λi​j1=λi​j2=0\lambda^{1}_{ij}=\lambda^{2}_{ij}=0 and λi​j3≠0\lambda^{3}_{ij}\neq 0, then the IGG is global U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1).

  3. (c)

    If λi​jμ≠0​∀μ\lambda^{\mu}_{ij}\neq 0\,\forall\,\mu, then the IGG is ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}.

Since the IGG is a gauge-invariant property of the Ansatz, it is conventional to label the Ansätze according to their IGG structure [e.g., U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) QSL, ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL, etc.], thereby identifying the type of emergent gauge theory associated with each QSL phase.

III Symmetries and projective realizations

III.1 Lattice and time-reversal symmetries

On the trellis lattice, any site can be described by the position vector 𝒓=x​𝑻1+y​𝑻2+ϵu\bm{r}=x\,\bm{T}_{1}+y\,\bm{T}_{2}+\bm{\epsilon}_{u}, where we choose the lattice vectors in the Cartesian basis as 𝑻1=a​𝑿^\bm{T}_{1}=a\hat{\bm{X}} and 𝑻2=(a/2)​𝑿^+(b+c)​𝒀^\bm{T}_{2}=(a/2)\hat{\bm{X}}+(b+c)\hat{\bm{Y}}, with aa, bb, and cc denoting the bond lengths as illustrated in Fig. 1. The vectors ϵu\bm{\epsilon}_{u} represent the positions of the sublattices within the unit cell. The unit cell consists of two sites located at ϵ1=(b/2)​𝒀^\bm{\epsilon}_{1}=(b/2)\hat{\bm{Y}} and ϵ2=−(b/2)​𝒀^\bm{\epsilon}_{2}=-(b/2)\hat{\bm{Y}}.

The symmetry group of the trellis lattice corresponds to the nonsymmorphic wallpaper group cmm, which can be generated by two translations (T1T_{1} and T2T_{2}), a twofold rotation (C2C_{2}), two mirror reflections (σx\sigma_{x} and σy\sigma_{y}), and two glide reflections (GxG_{x} and GyG_{y}). A pictorial representation of these symmetry elements is provided in Fig. 1(b). The action of each symmetry operation on a lattice site labeled by (x,y,u)(x,y,u)—where (x,y)(x,y) denotes the unit cell coordinate and uu specifies the sublattice index—is given by

T1​(x,y,u)→(x+1,y,u),T2​(x,y,u)→(x,y+1,u),C2​(x,y,u)→(−x,−y,u¯),σx​(x,y,u)→(x+y,−y,u¯),σy​(x,y,u)→(−x−y,y,u),Gx​(x,y,u)→(x+y,−y+1,u¯),Gy​(x,y,u)→(−x−y,y+1,u),\left.\begin{aligned} &T_{1}(x,y,u)\rightarrow(x+1,y,u),\\ &T_{2}(x,y,u)\rightarrow(x,y+1,u),\\ &C_{2}(x,y,u)\rightarrow(-x,-y,\bar{u}),\\ &\sigma_{x}(x,y,u)\rightarrow(x+y,-y,\bar{u}),\\ &\sigma_{y}(x,y,u)\rightarrow(-x-y,y,u),\\ &G_{x}(x,y,u)\rightarrow(x+y,-y+1,\bar{u}),\\ &G_{y}(x,y,u)\rightarrow(-x-y,y+1,u),\end{aligned}\right. (14)

with u¯≡3−u\bar{u}\equiv 3-u.

However, one can verify that several of these symmetry operations can be expressed in terms of a minimal generating set consisting of T2T_{2}, C2C_{2}, and σx\sigma_{x} as

T1=Gx2,Gx=T2σx,Gy=T22C2Gx,σy=C2σx.\left.\begin{aligned} &T_{1}=G_{x}^{2},\,\,G_{x}=T_{2}\sigma_{x},\,\,G_{y}=T_{2}^{2}C_{2}G_{x},\,\,\sigma_{y}=C_{2}\sigma_{x}.\end{aligned}\right. (15)

Therefore, the minimal set of generators required for constructing symmetric Ansätze invariant under the entire space group comprises T2T_{2}, C2C_{2}, and σx\sigma_{x}. Nonetheless, we include T1T_{1} in our analysis for convenience.

In addition to these lattice symmetries, we also incorporate time-reversal symmetry 𝒯\mathcal{T}, given our focus on classifying fully symmetric (i.e., nonchiral) spin liquid Ansätze. The time-reversal operation does not alter the spatial position of the lattice sites and hence, commutes with all space-group elements. However, its action on a mean-field Ansatz is nontrivial [69, 80] and is given by

𝒯⁡(ui​j,aμ)=−(ui​j,aμ).\mathcal{T}(u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij},a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mu})=-(u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij},a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mu}). (16)

Accordingly, the projective symmetry condition in Eq. (11) implies that the time-reversal symmetry imposes

G𝒯†​(i)​ui​j​G𝒯​(j)=−ui​j,for ​𝒪=𝒯.G_{\mathcal{T}}^{\dagger}(i)u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}G^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(j)=-u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij},\quad\text{for }\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{T}. (17)

Taken together with Eq. (14), this completely specifies the full symmetry group relevant for the trellis lattice.

Last, we note that there exist specific combinations of symmetry operations under which any given lattice site remains invariant. These combinations effectively act as the identity and are summarized below:

T1​T2​T1−1​T2−1\displaystyle T_{1}T_{2}T^{-1}_{1}T_{2}^{-1} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (18)
T1​C2−1​T1​C2\displaystyle T_{1}C_{2}^{-1}T_{1}C_{2} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (19)
T2​C2−1​T2​C2\displaystyle T_{2}C_{2}^{-1}T_{2}C_{2} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (20)
T1−1​σx−1​T1​σx\displaystyle T_{1}^{-1}\sigma_{x}^{-1}T_{1}\sigma_{x} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (21)
T1−1​T2​σx−1​T2​σx\displaystyle T_{1}^{-1}T_{2}\sigma_{x}^{-1}T_{2}\sigma_{x} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (22)
C2​σx​C2​σx\displaystyle C_{2}\sigma_{x}C_{2}\sigma_{x} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (23)
C22\displaystyle C_{2}^{2} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (24)
σx2\displaystyle\sigma_{x}^{2} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (25)
T1−1​T2​σx​T1​σx−1​T2−1\displaystyle T_{1}^{-1}T_{2}\sigma_{x}T_{1}\sigma_{x}^{-1}T_{2}^{-1} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (26)
C2​T1​T2−1​σx​C2​T2​σx\displaystyle C_{2}T_{1}T_{2}^{-1}\sigma_{x}C_{2}T_{2}\sigma_{x} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (27)
𝒯2\displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{2} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (28)
𝒯​𝒪​𝒯−1​𝒪−1\displaystyle\mathcal{T}\mathcal{O}\mathcal{T}^{-1}\mathcal{O}^{-1} =ℐ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{I}, (29)

where 𝒪∈{T1,T2,σx,C2}\mathcal{O}\in\{T_{1},T_{2},\sigma_{x},C_{2}\}.

III.2 Projective symmetry groups

To implement the projective realization of the symmetry elements 𝒪∈{T1,T2,σx,C2,𝒯}\mathcal{O}\in\{T_{1},T_{2},\sigma_{x},C_{2},\mathcal{T}\}, each symmetry operation must be associated with a corresponding SU(2) gauge transformation. These projective gauge transformations must satisfy the same algebraic relations as the original symmetry group generators. Consequently, the symmetry relations in Eqs. (18)–(29) impose a set of constraints on the operators W𝒪W_{\mathcal{O}}. The allowed PSG solutions are then obtained by solving the resulting algebraic conditions, as outlined in Appendix A. Different choices of the IGG lead to distinct classes of PSG solutions, which we describe below.

III.2.1 U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} solutions

Given that the trellis lattice is nonbipartite, SU(2) Ansätze with nonvanishing mean-field parameters on all nearest-neighbor bonds are not possible. We therefore begin with the IGG set to U(1), such that the identity element is defined up to a U(1) phase. Realizing such U(1) Ansätze requires including only hopping terms in the mean-field Hamiltonian introduced above.

The generic form of the PSG elements in this case is given by

W𝒪=ℱz​(ϕ𝒪​(x,y,u))​(i​τx)w𝒪,W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}=\mathcal{F}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}(x,y,u))(i\tau^{x})^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}}, (30)

where ℱz​(ξ)\mathcal{F}_{z}(\xi) ≡\equiv exp⁡(i​ξ​τz)\exp({i\xi\,\tau^{z}}) and w𝒪w_{\mathcal{O}} ∈\in {0,1}\{0,1\}. This structure ensures that the Ansätze are in their canonical form. Importantly, the symmetry relation in Eq. (22), where T1T_{1} appears only once, immediately excludes the possibility wT1w_{T_{1}} == 11. Therefore, only the two cases (wT1,wT2)=(0,0)(w_{T_{1}},w_{T_{2}})=(0,0) and (0,1)(0,1) are allowed for arbitrary values of wσxw_{\sigma_{x}}, wC2w_{C_{2}}, and w𝒯w_{\mathcal{T}}.

The algebraic PSG solutions are then given by the following expressions (see Appendix B for details):

Case I: wT1=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}=0, wT2=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}=0
ϕT1​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u) =y​θ,\displaystyle=y\,\theta, (31)
ϕT2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u) =0,\displaystyle=0, (32)
ϕC2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) =−(−1)wC2​(x​θC2​T1+y​θC2​T2)+ρC2,u,\displaystyle=-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}(x\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}+y\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}})+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (33)
ϕσx​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) =−(−1)wσx​(x​θσx​T1+y​θσx​T2)\displaystyle=-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}(x\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}+y\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}})
+(−1)wσx​12​y​(y−1)​θ+ρσx,u,\displaystyle\quad+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\frac{1}{2}y(y-1)\theta+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}, (34)
ϕ𝒯​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y,u) =y​θ𝒯​T2+ρ𝒯,u.\displaystyle=y\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{2}}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T},u}. (35)
Case II: wT1=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}=0, wT2=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}=1
ϕT1​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u) =(−1)y​θ,\displaystyle=(-1)^{y}\theta, (36)
ϕT2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u) =0,\displaystyle=0, (37)
ϕC2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) =(−1)wC2​(ζy​θC2​T2)+ρC2,u,\displaystyle=(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}(\zeta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}})+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (38)
ϕσx​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) =(−1)wσx​(ζy​θσx​T2−y​θ)+ρσx,u,\displaystyle=(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}(\zeta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}-y\,\theta)+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}, (39)
ϕ𝒯​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y,u) =ζy​θ𝒯​T2+ρ𝒯,u,\displaystyle=\zeta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}\,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{2}}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T},u}, (40)

where ζy=12​(1+(−1)y)\zeta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}=\frac{1}{2}(1+(-1)^{y}).

All allowed U(1) phase parameters θ\theta and ρ\rho for each choice of {wT2,wσx,wC2,w𝒯}\{w_{T_{2}},w_{\sigma_{x}},w_{C_{2}},w_{\mathcal{T}}\} are enumerated in Table 1. Thus, any U(1) PSG solution can be uniquely identified by three binary integers {wC2,wσx,w𝒯}\{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}},w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}},w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}\} and nine U(1) phases: {θ,θC2​T1,θC2​T2,θσx​T1,θσx​T2,θ𝒯​T2,ρC2,u,ρσx,u,ρ𝒯,u},\left\{\theta,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}},\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}},\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}},\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}},\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{2}},\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u},\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u},\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T},u}\right\}, each taking values in [0,2​π)[0,2\pi). However, these parameters are not all independent due to gauge redundancy. The gauge-inequivalent combinations of θ\theta and ρ\rho for various choices of {wC2,wσx,w𝒯}\{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}},w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}},w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}\} are summarized in Table 1, enlisting a total of 448 distinct U(1) PSGs. Hence, the full symmetry group of the trellis lattice admits 448 inequivalent U(1) projective symmetry group realizations.

III.2.2 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} solutions

Breaking down the IGG from U(1) to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} necessitates the inclusion of both hopping and pairing amplitudes in the link fields, thereby requiring the most general form of mean-field Ansätze. Within this framework, projective realizations of the symmetry group are defined up to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge transformations, i.e., global signs ±1\pm 1. Solving the associated algebraic constraints (see Appendix C), we obtain a total of 256 gauge-inequivalent ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG solutions. These can be summarized as follows:

WT1​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u) =ηT1y​τ0,\displaystyle=\eta_{T_{1}}^{\,y}\tau^{0}, (41)
WT2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u) =τ0,\displaystyle=\tau^{0}, (42)
WC2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) =ηC2​T2y​ηT1x​𝒲C2,u,\displaystyle=\eta_{C_{2}T_{2}}^{\,y}\eta_{T_{1}}^{\,x}\mathcal{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (43)
Wσx​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) =ηT1−y(y−1)/2+xηuσxτ0,\displaystyle=\eta_{T_{1}}^{\,-y(y-1)/2+x}\eta^{u}_{\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}, (44)
W𝒯​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y,u) =η𝒯​yy​𝒲𝒯,u,\displaystyle=\eta^{\,y}_{\mathcal{T}y}\mathcal{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T},u}, (45)

where all the parameters η…\eta_{\ldots} take values ±1\pm 1. The sublattice-dependent PSG elements 𝒲C2,u\mathcal{W}_{C_{2},u} and 𝒲𝒯,u∈\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{T},u}\in SU(2) are naturally constrained by the gauge-enriched algebraic relations imposed by the symmetry group. All gauge-inequivalent choices for these sublattice-dependent elements are provided in Table 2. From the enumeration therein, we see that when the IGG is set to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, the full symmetry group admits 256 distinct projective realizations.

IV Short-ranged mean-field Ansätze

Given the PSG solutions obtained in Secs. III.2.1 and III.2.2, we now turn to the construction of mean-field Ansätze for QSL states by imposing symmetry constraints on the link fields. The detailed derivation of symmetry-allowed forms for the link variables is presented in Appendix D. While our algebraic analysis yielded 448 U(1) and 256 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG classes, the number of distinct realizable short-ranged Ansätze on the trellis lattice is significantly fewer. This reduction arises from restricting the link fields to nonzero values on only the three symmetry-inequivalent nearest-neighbor bonds—JhJ_{h}, JvJ_{v}, and JzJ_{z}.

Within this short-range framework, we find a total of 6+16+1 U(1) Ansätze, where “+1+1” corresponds to an infinite class of gauge-inequivalent states stemming from a continuous U(1) degree of freedom associated with the PSG class given in the second row of Table 1. Additionally, we identify 25 distinct ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze. In this section, we present and discuss the structure and classification of these short-ranged mean-field states.

Before proceeding further, it is useful to introduce an SU(2) flux operator, which provides additional gauge-invariant characterization of the Ansätze, beyond the PSG labels. Defined for a closed loop 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} based at site ii, the SU(2) flux or loop operator is given by

𝒫𝒞i=ui​j​uj​l​…​uk​i.\mathcal{P}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}=u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{jl}\ldots u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ki}. (46)

Under a local SU(2) gauge transformation WiW_{i}, this operator transforms as

𝒫𝒞i→Wi†​𝒫𝒞i​Wi,\mathcal{P}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}\rightarrow W^{\dagger}_{i}\mathcal{P}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}, (47)

implying that the commutation or anticommutation relations between loop operators based at the same site remain invariant under such a rotation. Hence, the flux structure around various plaquettes becomes a powerful tool to distinguish between different Ansätze.

In general, a loop operator around a qq-sided plaquette takes the form [80]

P𝒞i​(φ𝒞i)∝gi​ℱz​(i​φ𝒞i)​(τz)q​gi†,gi∈SU⁡(2),P^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}(\varphi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}})\propto g^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\mathcal{F}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(i\varphi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{C}_{i}})(\tau^{z})^{q}g_{i}^{\dagger},\quad g^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\in\mathrm{SU}(2), (48)

where φ𝒞i\varphi_{\mathcal{C}_{i}} represents the effective flux piercing the loop 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i}.

On the trellis lattice, we consider a representative base site, labeled as “1” without loss of generality, as shown in Figs. 2(a) and 2(b). Starting from this site, we define one hexagonal loop PhP_{h}, one square loop PsP_{s}, and two triangular loops Pt1P_{t_{1}} and Pt2P_{t_{2}}, each associated with fluxes φh\varphi_{h}, φs\varphi_{s}, φt1\varphi_{t_{1}}, and φt2\varphi_{t_{2}}, respectively. In the case of a U(1) IGG, these fluxes commute, and their additive structure permits the identification of the total flux threading a hexagonal plaquette as the sum of the fluxes through its constituent triangular and square subloops. The corresponding flux configurations for each U(1) Ansatz are illustrated in Fig. 3.

IV.1 U(1) Ansätze

In this section, we present the different symmetric U(1) mean-field Ansätze that are realizable under the constraint of having nonzero mean-field amplitudes only on the three types of nearest-neighbor bonds.

We classify the Ansätze into four distinct classes—A, B, C, and D—based on the flux ϕh\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{h} threading the hexagonal plaquette (θ=0\theta=0 or π\pi), and the spatial modulation of the mean-field amplitudes, which determines whether the unit cell must be enlarged. All the U(1) Ansätze are graphically illustrated in Fig. 3 and the corresponding PSGs are enlisted in appendix (Table  9).

IV.1.1 Class A

Class A Ansätze are characterized by a vanishing flux through the hexagonal plaquettes, i.e., ϕh=0\phi_{h}=0. There are two U(1) Ansätze in this class. The labeling of the bonds is defined in Fig. 2(c), and the graphical representations of these Ansätze are provided in Figs. 3(a) and 3(b).

These Ansätze can be further distinguished by the fluxes threading the square and triangular loops. In the U1 family, all loop fluxes vanish, i.e., ϕs=0\phi_{s}=0 and (ϕt1,ϕt2)=(0,0)(\phi_{t_{1}},\phi_{t_{2}})=(0,0). In contrast, the U2 states are characterized by ϕs=π\phi_{s}=\pi and (ϕt1,ϕt2)=(0,π)(\phi_{t_{1}},\phi_{t_{2}})=(0,\pi).

IV.1.2 Class B

Class B Ansätze feature a π\pi-flux through the hexagonal plaquettes, i.e., ϕh=π\phi_{h}=\pi. Their realization necessitates a doubling of the unit cell along the T1T_{1} direction, due to sign-alternating mean-field amplitudes on the zigzag bonds. Explicitly, denoting the zigzag bonds within the (x,y)(x,y) unit cell as uz​(x,y)u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(x,y) and uz′​(x,y)u^{\prime}_{z}(x,y), their modulation follows:

uz​(x,y)\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(x,y) =(−1)x​uz,\displaystyle=(-1)^{x}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}, (49)
uz′​(x,y)\displaystyle u^{\prime}_{z}(x,y) =(−1)x​uz′.\displaystyle=(-1)^{x}u^{\prime}_{z}. (50)

This class contains two Ansätze, labeled U3 and U4, illustrated in Fig. 3(c) and 3(d), respectively. For U3, ϕs=π\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s}=\pi and (ϕt1,ϕt2)=(0,0)(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{1}},\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{2}})=(0,0), whereas for U4, ϕs=0\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s}=0 and (ϕt1,ϕt2)=(0,π)(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{1}},\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{2}})=(0,\pi).

IV.1.3 Class C

Class C Ansätze also exhibit zero flux through the hexagonal plaquettes, but differ from class A in the spatial modulation of the amplitudes. In this case, the unit cell is doubled along the T2T_{2} direction, with the mean-field amplitudes modulated as

uv,h,z​(x,y)\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{v,h,z}(x,y) =(−1)y​uv,h,z,\displaystyle=(-1)^{y}u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{v,h,z}, (51)
uh,z′​(x,y)\displaystyle u^{\prime}_{h,z}(x,y) =(−1)y​uh,z′,\displaystyle=(-1)^{y}u^{\prime}_{h,z}, (52)
aμ,u′\displaystyle a^{\prime}_{\mu,u} =(−1)y​aμ,u.\displaystyle=(-1)^{y}a_{\mu,u}. (53)

This class includes two Ansätze, labeled U5 and U6, depicted in Fig. 3(e) and 3(f). For U5, the square flux vanishes and the triangular fluxes alternate with the unit cell’s position along T2T_{2}: (ϕt1,ϕt2)=(0,π)(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{1}},\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{2}})=(0,\pi) or (π,0)(\pi,0). For U6, ϕs=π\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{s}=\pi, and (ϕt1,ϕt2)=(0,0)(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{1}},\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{t_{2}})=(0,0) or (π,π)(\pi,\pi) depending on the T2T_{2} position.

IV.1.4 Class D

In Class D, the size of the unit cell depends on the value of the phase θ∉{0,π}\theta\notin\{0,\pi\}. While the amplitudes on the JvJ_{v} and JhJ_{h} bonds remain translationally invariant, the zigzag bond amplitudes vary spatially as

uz​(x,y)\displaystyle u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(x,y) =ℱz​(−x​θ)​uz,\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(-x\theta)u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}, (54)
uz′​(x,y)\displaystyle u^{\prime}_{z}(x,y) =ℱz​(−x​θ)​uz′,\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(-x\theta)u^{\prime}_{z}, (55)

where, as before, ℱz​(ξ)=exp⁡(i​ξ​τz)\mathcal{F}_{z}(\xi)=\exp({i\xi\tau^{z}}). This modulation is periodic only when θ=p​π/q\theta=p\pi/q for integers pp and qq. The corresponding Ansatz then requires an enlarged unit cell of size qq along T1T_{1}. For example, θ=π/3\theta=\pi/3 implies a tripled unit cell, while θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4 requires quadrupling.

The associated flux through the hexagonal loop is ϕh=p​π/q\phi_{h}=p\pi/q, which is one realization of the U1qp{}^{p}_{q} PSGs, leading to an infinite number of U1qp{}^{p}_{q} Ansätze [69]. As the horizontal bond amplitudes vanish in these Ansätze, no square or triangular fluxes exist. Although the resulting fluxes differ from 00 or π\pi — the usual values for time-reversal–invariant hoppings with real amplitudes— these fractional fluxes, in appropriate gauges, alternate in sign between up and down spins, thereby preserving time-reversal symmetry [80]. It is worth noting that a chiral spin liquid is realized when nontrivial (not 00 or π\pi) fluxes thread odd-sided loops.

IV.2 ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze

All gauge-inequivalent Ansätze with IGG≃ℤ2\mathrm{IGG}\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{2} are enumerated in Table 3, yielding a total of 25 distinct ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} mean-field Ansätze.

The emergence of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze, as descendants from different parent states, can occur through two mechanisms: (1) the first route involves adding symmetry-allowed pairing terms to an existing U(1) Ansatz, thereby modifying the IGG from U(1) to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}; (2) alternatively, ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze can be obtained via directly breaking the symmetry down from an SU(2) IGG to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}. The associated PSGs are tabulated in Table  10. In this case, two distinct SU(2) parent states are possible, characterized by 00- and π\pi-flux threading the hexagonal plaquettes. These states feature vanishing mean-field amplitudes on the horizontal bonds and are continuously connected to the 00- and π\pi-flux SU(2) spin liquids previously studied on the honeycomb lattice [112, 77].

Out of all the possible PSG solutions, No. 17 and No. 8 Ansätze arise from the PSG classes corresponding to the second and fifth rows of Table 2, respectively. The remaining PSG classes do not permit a full reduction of the SU(2) IGG down to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, and thus do not yield viable ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids within our short-range framework. The Z1 state in Table 3 corresponds to the nonprojective (linear) representation of the space group with ss-wave hoppings and pairings, and is a fully gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSL.

The last column of Table 3 documents the U(1) or SU(2) parent state from which each ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansatz descends. Entries labeled with “A” refer to the SU(2) π\pi-flux state, which are obtained via mechanism (2).

V Quantum spin liquid phases

It is important to note that the PSG classification and the subsequent analysis of mean-field band structures address a question that is logically distinct from energetic stabilization in a specific microscopic Hamiltonian. The PSG framework enumerates all symmetry-allowed quantum spin liquid Ansätze on the trellis lattice, independent of their variational energies, and thereby identifies the full landscape of possible fractionalized phases. Within this space, the semi-Dirac spin liquid emerges as a distinct symmetry-allowed state characterized by a linear-quadratic spinon dispersion at high-symmetry points in the Brillouin zone. Whether such a state is realized as the ground state of a particular spin Hamiltonian is a separate, model-dependent question that requires energetic optimization or unbiased numerical methods. In the present work, we find that the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model on the trellis lattice does not energetically stabilize the semi-Dirac spin liquid, which therefore remains a phase realized at the level of PSG classification and mean-field parameter space rather than in the optimized phase diagram of the physical spin model. This distinction is generic to PSG-based studies and does not diminish the conceptual significance of the semi-Dirac spin liquid as a symmetry-allowed quantum spin liquid with characteristic universal properties. This separation between PSG classification and energetic selection is standard in parton-based approaches [69, 78, 113].

The properties of the Ansätze identified above depend on the choice of mean-field parameters, which are, in turn, determined by minimizing the energy with respect to a specific Hamiltonian. Consequently, the physical characteristics of each Ansatz are inherently model dependent. In this section, however, instead of initially focusing on such microscopic details, we choose to first analyze the general features of the six U(1) Ansätze. Thereafter, we relate these findings to the physics of the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model with Jh−Jv−JzJ_{h}-J_{v}-J_{z} couplings via a fully self-consistent calculation.

V.1 Mean-field phase diagrams

The unit cell of the trellis lattice contains three inequivalent bonds, each characterized by a hopping amplitude: χh\chi_{h}, χv\chi_{v}, and χz\chi_{z}. By independently varying these parameters, we uncover a rich variety of phases, including both gapped and gapless states exhibiting Fermi surfaces (FSs), nodal lines, semi-Dirac and Dirac points. We now present a detailed discussion of these phases for all six U(1) Ansätze as well as their associated band structures. For clarity, we set χh=1\chi_{h}=1 throughout the analysis.

Among the six U(1) Ansätze, the U1 family exhibits the most intricate phase diagram, as shown in Fig. 4(a). Specifically, we observe extended windows of Dirac spin liquid (DSL), FS, and gapped phases, delineated in the parameter space defined by χz\chi_{z} and χv\chi_{v}. Each phase is distinguished by its band structure and excitation spectrum near the Fermi energy, illustrated in Fig. 4(d) for representative parameter values marked by colored dots in the phase diagram. Here, the phase boundary between the DSL and FS phases is specified by χv=−2​χz+χz2,\chi_{v}=-2\chi_{z}+\chi_{z}^{2}, while the boundary between the FS and gapped phases is given by χv=2+χz+χz2/8.\chi_{v}=2+\chi_{z}+{\chi_{z}^{2}}/{8}.

Additional noteworthy features appear at the DSL’s boundaries. For instance, the blue circle at χv=0\chi_{v}=0 marks a nodal-line spin liquid phase. Moreover, along a segment of the line χv\chi_{v} == 2​χz2\chi_{z}, we find a semi-Dirac spin liquid (labeled s-DSL) [114]. In this semi-Dirac phase, the bands touch at the point K3K_{3} == (0,2​π/3)(0,2\pi/3), at which the dispersion is linear along one momentum direction and quadratic along the orthogonal one11 1 Interestingly, similar band structures also appear in other contexts [115] including in studies of Kitaev spin liquids [116], and topological materials [117, 118, 119, 120].. Consequently, quasiparticles are effectively massive in one direction, while exhibiting massless Dirac-like behavior in the other. Notably, the semi-Dirac point acts as a precursor to the Dirac points that characterize the DSL phase (as discussed in Sec. V.2 below; see also Fig. 5). Here, we note that this U1 Ansatz includes the semi-Dirac dispersion observed in the tight-binding honeycomb model of Refs. [121, 122]. This connection is established by including further-neighbor amplitudes on the trellis lattice –namely, the diagonal links within the square plaquettes and the longest vertical link within the hexagonal plaquette –in addition to those shown in Fig. 3(a). The s-DSL nodes emerge when χv=χz=χ\chi_{v}=\chi_{z}=\chi, χh=0\chi_{h}=0, and the hopping amplitude on these further-neighbor links is set to χ/3\chi/3. The DSL, FS, s-DSL, and gapped phases all meet at a multicritical point (χv,χz)=(8,4)(\chi_{v},\chi_{z})=(8,4).

Proceeding along the same lines, the phase diagram for the U2 Ansatz is shown in Fig. 4(b). It features two gapped phases separated by a gapless Dirac spin liquid phase, which lies along the line χv\chi_{v} == 2​χz\sqrt{2}\chi_{z}. Representative band structures at selected points of this phase diagram are displayed in Fig. 4(e). In this case, the Dirac point lies along the momentum path between the K2=(2​π/3,2​π/3)K_{2}=(2\pi/3,2\pi/3) and K3K_{3} points in reciprocal space.

Next, Fig. 4(c) showcases the phase diagram for the U3 Ansatz. At χv=0\chi_{v}=0, this exhibits a nodal-line phase, with the nodal line itself stretching between K1′=(0,π/6)K_{1}^{\prime}=(0,\pi/6) and K2′=(0,π/2)K_{2}^{\prime}=(0,\pi/2). Upon increasing χv\chi_{v}, a Dirac spin liquid appears but with a tilted cone located along the path between K2′K_{2}^{\prime} and K3′=(π/3,π/2)K_{3}^{\prime}=(\pi/3,\pi/2),  [123, 124]. As χv\chi_{v} is increased even further, an s-DSL phase emerges that subsequently transitions into a gapped phase. The semi-Dirac spin liquid located along the line χv=2​χz\chi_{v}=\sqrt{2}\chi_{z} thus separates the DSL and gapped phases. It is characterized by a linear-quadratic dispersion centered at K3′K_{3}^{\prime}, and the tilted Dirac cone of the DSL phase in fact originates from the semi-Dirac point (see Sec. V.2 below). The corresponding band structures are all plotted in Fig. 4(f).

Similarly, the U4 Ansatz’s phase diagram is shown in Fig. 4(g). It comprises two distinct gapped phases separated by a semi-Dirac spin liquid phase (black line) occurring, as before, along χv=2​χz\chi_{v}=\sqrt{2}\chi_{z}. The associated band structures are presented in Fig. 4(j). Unlike for the U1 Ansatz, the semi-Dirac point here does not split into a pair of Dirac points and the spectrum remains gapped on either side of the s-DSL; however, such a splitting could be induced by incorporating further-neighbor hopping terms.

Continuing with our sequence of U(1) QSLs, Fig. 4(h) presents the phase diagram for the U5 Ansatz, wherein a DSL region is enclosed between two gapped phases. The DSL phase is bounded by the curves

χv\displaystyle\chi_{v} =χz2​8−χz2\displaystyle=\frac{\chi_{z}}{2}\sqrt{8-\chi_{z}^{2}}\quad (for ​χz<2),\displaystyle(\text{for }\chi_{z}<2),
χv\displaystyle\chi_{v} =2,\displaystyle=2,\quad (for ​χz≥2),\displaystyle(\text{for }\chi_{z}\geq 2),
χv\displaystyle\chi_{v} =2​1+χz2.\displaystyle=2\sqrt{1+\chi_{z}^{2}}. (56)

At the boundary between the DSL and the gapped phase below it, we once again find semi-Dirac dispersion. The related band structures are illustrated in Fig. 4(k).

Finally, the phase diagram for the U6 Ansatz is shown in Fig. 4(i). The topology of the phase diagram closely resembles that for the U3 case, and an s-DSL phase separates the DSL and gapped phases. The phase boundaries for the semi-Dirac region are defined by

χv\displaystyle\chi_{v} =χz2​8+χz2\displaystyle=\frac{\chi_{z}}{2}\sqrt{8+\chi_{z}^{2}}\quad (for ​χz<2),\displaystyle(\text{for }\chi_{z}<2), (57)
χz\displaystyle\chi_{z} =12​4+χv2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{4+\chi_{v}^{2}}\quad (for ​χz≥2).\displaystyle(\text{for }\chi_{z}\geq 2). (58)

The associated spinon dispersions for this Ansatz are sketched in Fig. 4(l).

The s-DSL boundaries for all the Ansätze are tabulated in Table 4.

While our analysis of the semi-Dirac Ansätze has focused on a U(1) gauge structure, one can also realize ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} semi-Dirac Ansätze since their origin is rooted in the lattice (point group) symmetry.

V.2 Properties of the semi-Dirac spin liquid state

V.2.1 Origin and symmetry considerations

To better understand the transition from the DSL to the s-DSL identified above, we analyze the motion of the Dirac points in the Ansätze labeled U1, U3, U4, U5, and U6 in Fig. 3. As the hopping parameters are tuned, the Dirac points shift gradually in momentum space, as represented by the increasing intensity of color in Fig. 5. This continuous motion ultimately drives two distinct Dirac points to merge, giving rise to the s-DSL. Each pair of identically colored dots in Fig. 5 corresponds to a specific choice of hopping parameter close to the critical regime where the s-DSL emerges (see Fig. 4). The observations such as the number of s-DSL points within the extended Brillouin zone (EBZ) and the corresponding q-vectors connecting them (see Fig. 5) are summarised in Table 5.

In general, as underscored by Fig. 5, the merger of two Dirac nodes gives rise to a semi-Dirac node [91, 121]. Here, we demonstrate that a key requirement for this mechanism to work is that the little group at the band-touching momentum is the C2​vC_{2v} point group; i.e., it has twofold rotational symmetry and two orthogonal reflection planes. Let us consider a two-band Hamiltonian in the sublattice basis, which can be parameterized as

H⁡(𝒌)=a⁡(𝒌)​ς0+d→​(𝒌)⋅ς→,H(\bm{k})=a(\bm{k})\varsigma^{0}+\vec{d}(\bm{k})\cdot\vec{\varsigma}, (59)

where ς0\varsigma^{0} is the 2×22\times 2 identity matrix and ς→={ςx,ςy,ςz}\vec{\varsigma}=\{\varsigma^{x},\varsigma^{y},\varsigma^{z}\} are Pauli matrices that act on the two sublattices. The C2​vC_{2v} point group consists of two mirror reflections, σx\sigma_{x} and σy\sigma_{y}, and a C2C_{2} rotation. Under these operations, the Hamiltonian transforms as

𝒰𝒪​H​(𝒌)​𝒰𝒪†=H⁡(𝒪⁡(𝒌))for𝒪∈{Mx,My,C2},\mathcal{U}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{O}}H(\bm{k})\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}=H(\mathcal{O}(\bm{k}))\quad\text{for}\quad\mathcal{O}\in\{M^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x},M^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y},C^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}\}, (60)

with the corresponding sublattice transformation matrices

𝒰σx=ςx,𝒰σy=ς0,𝒰C2=ςx.\mathcal{U}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=\varsigma^{x},\quad\mathcal{U}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{y}}=\varsigma^{0},\quad\mathcal{U}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=\varsigma^{x}. (61)

The σx\sigma_{x} symmetry constrains the Hamiltonian’s coefficients as follows:

dx​(kx,−ky)\displaystyle d_{x}(k_{x},-k_{y}) =dx​(kx,ky),\displaystyle=d_{x}(k_{x},k_{y}),
dy​(kx,−ky)\displaystyle d_{y}(k_{x},-k_{y}) =−dy​(kx,ky),\displaystyle=-d_{y}(k_{x},k_{y}),
dz​(kx,−ky)\displaystyle d_{z}(k_{x},-k_{y}) =−dz​(kx,ky),\displaystyle=-d_{z}(k_{x},k_{y}), (62)

implying that dx​(𝒌)d_{x}(\bm{k}) is even in kyk_{y}, while dy​(𝒌)d_{y}(\bm{k}) and dz​(𝒌)d_{z}(\bm{k}) are odd in kyk_{y}. Similarly, for 𝒪=σy\mathcal{O}=\sigma_{y}, Eq. (59) yields H⁡(−kx,ky)=H⁡(kx,ky)H(-k_{x},k_{y})=H(k_{x},k_{y}), implying that all components of d→​(𝒌)\vec{d}(\bm{k}) are even in kxk_{x}. The C2C_{2} operation imposes no additional constraints since C2=σx​σyC_{2}=\sigma_{x}\sigma_{y}. The scalar function a⁡(𝒌)a(\bm{k}) is always even in both kxk_{x} and kyk_{y}.

With these symmetry constraints in place, we construct a minimal model that yields a semi-Dirac nodal structure. Keeping only the leading symmetry-allowed terms consistent with a single mirror-protected linear dispersion along kyk_{y}, we choose

dx​(𝒌)\displaystyle d_{x}(\bm{k}) =m−m0​kx2,\displaystyle=m-m_{0}k_{x}^{2},
dy​(𝒌)\displaystyle d_{y}(\bm{k}) =v​ky,\displaystyle=vk_{y},
dz​(𝒌)\displaystyle d_{z}(\bm{k}) =a⁡(𝒌)=0.\displaystyle=a(\bm{k})=0. (63)

The resulting minimal Hamiltonian is

H⁡(𝒌)=(m−m0​kx2)​σx+v​ky​σy,H(\bm{k})=(m-m_{0}k_{x}^{2})\sigma^{x}+vk_{y}\sigma^{y}, (64)

with spectrum

E⁡(𝒌)=±v2​ky2+(m−m0​kx2)2.E(\bm{k})=\pm\sqrt{v^{2}k_{y}^{2}+(m-m_{0}k_{x}^{2})^{2}}. (65)

For m0>0m_{0}>0, there exist three distinct regimes:

  1. 1.

    mm >> 00: Two Dirac nodes appear at kyk_{y} == 00 and kx=±k0=±m/m0k_{x}=\pm k_{0}=\pm\sqrt{m/m_{0}}. Expanding around kx=±k0k_{x}=\pm k_{0} yields m−m0​(k0+δ​kx)2≈−2​m0​k0​δ​kxm-m_{0}(k_{0}+\delta k_{x})^{2}\approx-2m_{0}k_{0}\delta k_{x}, showing that each node is a Dirac point with velocities (vx,vy)=(2​m0​k0,v)(v_{x},v_{y})=(2m_{0}k_{0},v).

  2. 2.

    m=0m=0: The two Dirac nodes merge, producing the dispersion

    E⁡(𝒌)\displaystyle E(\bm{k}) =±v2​ky2+m02​kx4∼±v​ky,±m0​kx2.\displaystyle=\pm\sqrt{v^{2}k_{y}^{2}+m^{2}_{0}k_{x}^{4}}\sim\pm vk_{y},\,\,\pm m_{0}k_{x}^{2}. (66)

    At m=0m=0, the two Dirac cones merge into a semi-Dirac node, exhibiting quadratic dispersion along kxk_{x} and linear dispersion along kyk_{y}.

  3. 3.

    m<0m<0: No nodal points exist, and a gap opens.

This minimal model thus captures the essential mechanism underlying the transition from a Dirac spin liquid to a gapped spin liquid through an intermediate semi-Dirac spin liquid. In particular, this mechanism accounts for the transitions observed in the U1, U3, U5, and U6 Ansätze.

In contrast, higher little-group symmetries such as C3​vC_{3v}, C4​vC_{4v}, or C6​vC_{6v} are incompatible with the realization of semi-Dirac dispersions. To illustrate this, let us focus on C4​vC_{4v}. In this case, the presence of a term such as v​ky​σyvk_{y}\sigma^{y} would, by virtue of C4C_{4} rotational symmetry, require the existence of an equivalent linear term along the kxk_{x} direction, thereby enforcing full Dirac-like dispersions in both momentum directions. To formalize this argument, we generalize the matrices 𝒰𝒪\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{O}} to pseudospin representations. These pseudospin matrices must be consistent with how the underlying physical degrees of freedom (e.g., spin, orbital, sublattice) transform under the operations of the point group, while simultaneously respecting the group multiplication rules (up to projective phases). For C4​vC_{4v}, the symmetry group is generated by σx\sigma_{x} and C4C_{4}, for which we adopt the representation

𝒰σx=ςx,𝒰C4=ι˙​eι˙​π4​ςz.\mathcal{U}_{\sigma_{x}}=\varsigma^{x},\quad\mathcal{U}_{C_{4}}=\dot{\iota}e^{\dot{\iota}\frac{\pi}{4}\varsigma^{z}}. (67)

Since 𝒰σx\mathcal{U}_{\sigma_{x}} coincides with the choice made in the C2​vC_{2v} case, it imposes the same constraints as Eq. (62), leading to the low-energy expansion

dx​(𝒌)\displaystyle d_{x}(\bm{k}) =ax​kx+bx​ky2+O⁡(kx2)+O⁡(ky4),\displaystyle=a_{x}k_{x}+b_{x}k_{y}^{2}+O(k_{x}^{2})+O(k_{y}^{4}),
dy​(𝒌)\displaystyle d_{y}(\bm{k}) =by​ky+O⁡(ky3),\displaystyle=b_{y}k_{y}+O(k_{y}^{3}),
dz​(𝒌)\displaystyle d_{z}(\bm{k}) =bz​ky+O⁡(ky3).\displaystyle=b_{z}k_{y}+O(k_{y}^{3}). (68)

The additional constraints from C4C_{4} symmetry read

dx​(−ky,kx)\displaystyle d_{x}(-k_{y},k_{x}) =−dy​(kx,ky),\displaystyle=-d_{y}(k_{x},k_{y}),
dy​(−ky,kx)\displaystyle d_{y}(-k_{y},k_{x}) =dx​(kx,ky),\displaystyle=d_{x}(k_{x},k_{y}),
dz​(−ky,kx)\displaystyle d_{z}(-k_{y},k_{x}) =dz​(kx,ky).\displaystyle=d_{z}(k_{x},k_{y}). (69)

The first two conditions enforce ax=bya_{x}=b_{y}, while simultaneously requiring dz=0d_{z}=0. Consequently, the presence of a linear by​kyb_{y}k_{y} term in dyd_{y} necessitates the appearance of an equivalent by​kxb_{y}k_{x} term in dxd_{x}. This enforces linear dispersions along both momentum directions, thereby ruling out the semi-Dirac scenario. An analogous argument applies to other little groups with higher symmetries, such as C6​vC_{6v}. We thus conclude that C2​vC_{2v} constitutes a special case: It provides precisely the symmetry constraints necessary to stabilize semi-Dirac nodes, whereas higher point-group symmetries inevitably restore full Dirac dispersions.

V.2.2 Spin-spin correlation functions

Having established the origin of the s-DSL state, we now turn to its correlation functions. To compute equal-time spin-spin correlations, it is convenient to rewrite the spins using the Abrikosov-fermion representation of Eq. (2). In this formulation, the Heisenberg exchange becomes a four-fermion term, which we decouple at the mean-field level in the hopping channel, yielding a quadratic spinon Hamiltonian. Diagonalizing this mean-field Hamiltonian gives the spinon eigenmodes ψn​(i)\psi_{n}(i) and their energies. The mean-field ground state is then obtained by filling the lowest half of these modes, from which we construct the single-particle Green’s function Gi​j=∑n∈occψn∗​(i)​ψn​(j)G_{ij}=\sum_{n\in{\rm occ}}\psi_{n}^{\ast}(i)\psi_{n}(j). Wick’s theorem allows us to express the physical spin–spin correlator entirely in terms of Gi​jG_{ij} as ⟨𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j⟩∼−|Gi​j|2\langle\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{i}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{\hat{S}}_{j}\rangle\sim-|G_{ij}|^{2}, so that the spatial decay of the spin correlations follows directly from the numerically evaluated |Gi​j|2|G_{ij}|^{2}.

Figure 6 presents the real-space decay of the spin-spin correlations for the U1 Ansatz in the s-DSL phase with hopping parameters χh=1.0\chi_{h}=1.0, χv=9.0\chi_{v}=9.0, and χz=4.5\chi_{z}=4.5 (see Figs. 3 and 4). In panel (a), the radius of the black disks represents the correlation strength, while the colored vertical and horizontal lines indicate the directions analyzed in panels (b) and (c). Panel (b) shows that correlations along the vertical (yy) direction decay with exponent ≈3\approx 3, whereas panel (c) demonstrates that correlations along the two horizontal cuts decay much more rapidly, with exponent ≈6\approx 6.

These exponents could be understood as follows. In the long-wavelength limit, the dispersion of the s-DSL can be approximated as

E⁡(𝒌)=m​k12+k2.E(\bm{k})=mk^{2}_{1}+k_{2}. (70)

The corresponding low-energy effective theory is obtained by adding a quadratic anisotropic term (mass) to the massless Dirac Lagrangian in (1+1)(1+1)D:

ℒ=ψ¯(iγμ∂μ−m∂12)ψ,\mathcal{L}=\bar{\psi}\left(i\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}-m\,\partial_{1}^{2}\right)\psi, (71)

where μ=0,2\mu=0,2 and ψ¯=γ0​ψ†\bar{\psi}=\gamma^{0}\psi^{\dagger}. In (2+1)(2+1)D, the Green’s function satisfies

(iγμ∂μ−m∂12)𝒢(𝒓−𝒓′)=δ3(𝒓−𝒓′).\left(i\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}-m\,\partial_{1}^{2}\right)\mathcal{G}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})=\delta^{3}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime}). (72)

Here, we temporarily use the notation 𝒓≡(r0,r1,r2)\bm{r}\equiv(r_{0},r_{1},r_{2}) to denote a three-vector in which the first component is a time coordinate and the other two are Cartesian coordinates. Using the Fourier transform

𝒢⁡(𝒓−𝒓′)=∫d3​𝒌(2​π)3​ei​𝒌⋅(𝒓−𝒓′)​G​(𝒌),\mathcal{G}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})=\int\frac{d^{3}\bm{k}}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})}G(\bm{k}), (73)

we obtain the Green’s function in momentum space:

G⁡(𝒌)=1γμ​kμ+m​k12=γμ​kμ−m​k12kμ2−m2​k14.G(\bm{k})=\frac{1}{\gamma^{\mu}k_{\mu}+mk^{2}_{1}}=\frac{\gamma^{\mu}k_{\mu}-mk^{2}_{1}}{k^{2}_{\mu}-m^{2}k^{4}_{1}}. (74)

To analyze the spatial decay of correlations, we consider the real-space Green’s function 𝒢⁡(𝒓)\mathcal{G}(\bm{r}), obtained by Fourier transforming over spatial components:

𝒢⁡(𝒓)=∫d2​q​d​k1(2​π)3​ei​𝒌⋅𝒓​γμ​qμ−m​k12qμ2−m2​k14,\mathcal{G}(\bm{r})=\int\frac{d^{2}q\,dk_{1}}{(2\pi)^{3}}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{r}}\frac{\gamma^{\mu}q_{\mu}-mk^{2}_{1}}{q^{2}_{\mu}-m^{2}k^{4}_{1}}, (75)

where 𝒌=(q0,k1,q2)\bm{k}=(q_{0},k_{1},q_{2}) separates the μ=0,2\mu=0,2 components [the (1+1)(1+1)D Dirac piece] from the anisotropic momentum k1k_{1}.

We can now carry out a simple scaling analysis that proves informative. In order to ascertain the asymptotic behavior of 𝒢⁡(x,y)\mathcal{G}(x,y) at large distances, we employ the anisotropic scaling: r0∼r~0​Λr_{0}\sim\tilde{r}_{0}\Lambda, r1∼r~1​Λ1/2r_{1}\sim\tilde{r}_{1}\Lambda^{1/2}, and r2∼r~2​Λr_{2}\sim\tilde{r}_{2}\Lambda. With the rescaling k0→k~0/Λk_{0}\to\tilde{k}_{0}/\Lambda, k1→k~1/Λ1/2k_{1}\to\tilde{k}_{1}/\Lambda^{1/2}, and k2→k~2/Λk_{2}\to\tilde{k}_{2}/\Lambda, Eq. (75) becomes

𝒢(Λr~0,Λ1/2r~1,Λr~2)=Λ−3/2𝒢(r~0,r~1,r~2).\mathcal{G}(\Lambda\tilde{r}_{0},\Lambda^{1/2}\tilde{r}_{1},\Lambda\tilde{r}_{2})=\Lambda^{-3/2}\mathcal{G}(\tilde{r}_{0},\tilde{r}_{1},\tilde{r}_{2}). (76)

For equal-time correlations, we set r0=0r_{0}=0, yielding

𝒢(Λ1/2r~1,Λr~2)=Λ−3/2𝒢(r~1,r~2).\mathcal{G}(\Lambda^{1/2}\tilde{r}_{1},\Lambda\tilde{r}_{2})=\Lambda^{-3/2}\mathcal{G}(\tilde{r}_{1},\tilde{r}_{2}). (77)

The dependence along the two directions can then be straightforwardly extracted. Along r1r_{1}, we set r2=0r_{2}=0 and choose Λ=r12\Lambda=r^{2}_{1}, such that r~1=1\tilde{r}_{1}=1. This gives 𝒢⁡(r1,0)∼r1−3\mathcal{G}(r_{1},0)\sim r_{1}^{-3}. Likewise, along r2r_{2}, we set r1=0r_{1}=0 and choose Λ=r2\Lambda=r_{2}, such that r~2=1\tilde{r}_{2}=1; this shows that 𝒢(0,r2)∼r2−3/2\mathcal{G}(0,r_{2})\sim r_{2}^{-3/2}.

The equal-time correlator is defined as

𝒮+⁣−​(𝒓−𝒓′)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{+-}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime}) =⟨S+​(𝒓)​S−​(𝒓′)⟩\displaystyle=\langle S^{+}(\bm{r})S^{-}(\bm{r}^{\prime})\rangle
=⟨f↑†​(𝒓)​f↓​(𝒓)​f↓†​(𝒓′)​f↑​(𝒓′)⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle f^{\dagger}_{\uparrow}(\bm{r})f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\downarrow}(\bm{r})f^{\dagger}_{\downarrow}(\bm{r}^{\prime})f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\uparrow}(\bm{r}^{\prime})\right\rangle
=−⟨f↑†​(𝒓)​f↑​(𝒓′)⟩​⟨f↓†​(𝒓)​f↓​(𝒓′)⟩⋆,\displaystyle=-\left\langle f^{\dagger}_{\uparrow}(\bm{r})f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\uparrow}(\bm{r}^{\prime})\right\rangle\left\langle f^{\dagger}_{\downarrow}(\bm{r})f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\downarrow}(\bm{r}^{\prime})\right\rangle^{\star}, (78)

where, in the last step, we use Wick’s theorem. Defining the equal-time two-point correlator as 𝒢σ​(𝒓−𝒓′)=⟨fσ†​(𝒓)​fσ​(𝒓′)⟩\mathcal{G}_{\sigma}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})=\langle f^{\dagger}_{\sigma}(\bm{r})f^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma}(\bm{r}^{\prime})\rangle, we can write

𝒮+⁣−​(𝒓−𝒓′)=𝒢↑​(𝒓−𝒓′)​𝒢↓⋆​(𝒓−𝒓′).\mathcal{S}_{+-}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})=\mathcal{G}_{\uparrow}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})\mathcal{G}^{\star}_{\downarrow}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime}). (79)

By virtue of spin-rotation symmetry, this reduces to

𝒮+⁣−​(𝒓−𝒓′)=−|𝒢⁡(𝒓−𝒓′)|2,\mathcal{S}_{+-}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})=-|\mathcal{G}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})|^{2}, (80)

implying

𝒮+⁣−​(𝒓−𝒓′)∼{|r1−r1′|−6,if r2−r2′=0;|r2−r2′|−3,if r1−r1′=0.\mathcal{S}_{+-}(\bm{r}-\bm{r}^{\prime})\sim\begin{cases}|r_{1}-r^{\prime}_{1}|^{-6},&\text{if $r_{2}-r^{\prime}_{2}=0$;}\\ |r_{2}-r^{\prime}_{2}|^{-3},&\text{if $r_{1}-r^{\prime}_{1}=0$.}\end{cases} (81)

This reproduces the decay observed in Fig. 6. To fully capture all the fine oscillatory features of the spin–spin correlation function, it is necessary to evaluate the complete integral over the Brillouin zone in Eq. (75). A detailed analysis of this behavior is left for future work. We note that all along the phase boundary separating the DSL and gapped state shown in Fig.4(a), we realize a semi-Dirac spinon dispersion including at the multicritical point. These mean-field exponents should be compared with those in other gapless phases, such as a spinon Fermi surface state (∼r−3)(\sim r^{-3}) [125, 126, 127] and Dirac spin liquid (∼r−4)(\sim r^{-4}) [128]. Since the semi-Dirac dispersion originates from a merger of two Dirac cones that introduces a length scale, i.e., the inverse of the distance between the two Dirac cones, it would be interesting to explore how the ∼r−4\sim r^{-4} decay of the Dirac spin liquid transforms into the anisotropic exponents of the semi-Dirac state.

V.3 Ternary phase diagram of the Heisenberg model

Building on our analysis of the generic features of the Ansätze, we now investigate the phase diagram obtained from saddle-point solutions of a nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model with exchange couplings JvJ_{v} along the vertical ladder legs, JhJ_{h} along the horizontal rungs, and JzJ_{z} on the zigzag interladder bonds, as depicted in Fig. 1(a). The analysis is performed by self-consistently determining all mean-field amplitudes.

The saddle-point solutions of six U(1) Ansätze, considered up to a doubling of the unit cell, are summarized in Fig. 7. Within the ternary parameter space, six distinct phases (I–VI) emerge. The graphical representation in Fig. 7 directly highlights the saddle-point structures of the Ansätze, with bond widths scaled according to the self-consistently determined mean-field amplitudes at representative points.

  • •

    In phase I (blue), the amplitudes on the JvJ_{v} and JhJ_{h} bonds are negligible for all Ansätze, resulting in an effective 1D zigzag chain structure. A representative point here is (Jz,Jh,Jv)=(0.8,0.1,0.1)(J_{z},J_{h},J_{v})=(0.8,0.1,0.1) with optimized mean-field parameters (χz,χh,χv)(\chi_{z},\chi_{h},\chi_{v}) == (0.642,−0.009,0.003)(0.642,-0.009,0.003).

  • •

    In phase II (orange), realized by the Ansätze U2, U4, and U5 with 00- and π\pi-staggered fluxes through triangular plaquettes, the amplitudes on the legs dominate, producing an effective zigzag ladder structure. At the point (Jz,Jh,Jv)=(0.5,0.4,0.1)(J_{z},J_{h},J_{v})=(0.5,0.4,0.1), the optimized values are (0.583,0.352,−0.012)(0.583,0.352,-0.012).

  • •

    Phase III (green) corresponds to a rung-chain structure dominated by JhJ_{h} bonds, with negligible amplitudes on JvJ_{v} and JzJ_{z}. For couplings (Jz,Jh,Jv)(J_{z},J_{h},J_{v}) == (0.1,0.8,0.1)(0.1,0.8,0.1), the corresponding mean-field values are (0.001,0.636,0.013)(0.001,0.636,0.013).

  • •

    In phase IV (purple), a π\pi-flux rung-ladder state appears, realized by the U2, U3, and U6 Ansätze. For (0.1,0.6,0.3)(0.1,0.6,0.3), the optimized amplitudes are (0.000,0.630,0.192)(0.000,0.630,0.192).

  • •

    In phase V (pink), all Ansätze collapse to a ladder-dimer phase due to vanishingly small χz\chi_{z} and χh\chi_{h}. At (0.2,0.2,0.6)(0.2,0.2,0.6), the optimized parameters are (−0.004,−0.009,0.999)(-0.004,-0.009,0.999).

  • •

    Finally, at the junction of phases I, II, and V, a zero-flux honeycomb resonating-valence-bond-like state (phase VI) governs the low-energy behavior. Here, χh∼−0.009\chi_{h}\sim-0.009 is nearly zero, while (χz,χv)∼(0.636,−0.153)(\chi_{z},\chi_{v})\sim(0.636,-0.153). The relevant parent states include U1, U2, U5, and U6.

The isotropic point in the phase diagram, Jz=Jh=JvJ_{z}=J_{h}=J_{v} features a ladder-dimer state (phase V). In Fig. 8, we show the spinon-gap profile across the ternary phase diagram in Fig. 7. Although the effective low-energy states in phases (I) and (III)—which reduce to isolated one-dimensional chains—are expected to be gapless, we find a finite gap except at the special points Jv=Jh=0J_{v}=J_{h}=0 and Jz=Jv=0J_{z}=J_{v}=0 in these two phases, respectively. This is because, in addition to the dominant mean-field parameters χz\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z} and χh\chi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{h} in phases (I) and (III), respectively, the remaining mean-field parameters remain small but nonzero. As a result, a finite gap emerges.

In our self-consistent mean-field analysis, we also considered all ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze but found them either to be higher in energy than the corresponding U(1) states or to exhibit vanishing optimized pairing amplitudes (which are responsible for the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge structure in the first place), thereby flowing back to their parent U(1) states. It would be interesting to assess their variational energetics after Gutzwiller projection and investigate whether the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states are stabilized in some region of the phase diagram.

It is important to emphasize that the saddle-point phases described above assume full lattice and time-reversal symmetry. Certain paramagnetic phases, such as the Majumdar-Ghosh state [45], fall outside this fully symmetric framework. To capture these, one must consider symmetry-reduced versions of the Ansätze. For example, breaking σx\sigma_{x} yields a dimerized state with singlets on the zigzag bonds, corresponding to the Majumdar-Ghosh phase, which is twofold degenerate per zigzag ladder and is indicated in blue in Fig. 9. Similarly, breaking translational symmetry T1T_{1} gives rise to a rung-dimer phase with singlets on the horizontal rungs, also twofold degenerate per rung, shown in green in Fig. 9. The ladder-dimer phase remains stable within its domain. Overall, we identify three distinct dimerized quantum paramagnetic phases.

VI Spectral properties

To further characterize the quantum spin liquid states, we examine the time- and momentum-resolved spin-spin correlation function, namely, the DSF, defined as

𝒮μ​ν​(𝒒,ω)=∫d​τ​eι˙​ω​τ2​π​N​∑⟨i,j⟩eι˙​𝒒⋅(𝒓i−𝒓j)​⟨𝐒iμ​(τ)​𝐒jν​(0)⟩,\mathcal{S}^{\mu\nu}(\bm{q},\omega)=\int\frac{d\tau\,e^{\dot{\iota}\omega\tau}}{2\pi N}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}e^{\dot{\iota}\bm{q}\cdot(\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j})}\langle\mathbf{S}^{\mu}_{i}(\tau)\mathbf{S}^{\nu}_{j}(0)\rangle, (82)

with μ,ν=x,y,z\mu,\nu=x,y,z. The DSF is directly accessible in inelastic neutron scattering experiments and serves as a key probe of the spectral signatures of fractionalized excitations in QSLs.

In the following, we compute the DSF (and, where relevant, its frequency-integrated equal-time counterpart) using both mean-field theory (Figs. 10 and 11) and beyond-mean-field approaches (Fig. 12), including Keldysh pf-FRG and DMRG.

Before presenting the results, we clarify the scope of the comparison between mean-field and numerical approaches. We emphasize that the dynamical structure factors computed from the fermionic mean-field Ansätze should be interpreted as qualitative probes of the underlying parton band structures rather than as quantitative predictions for the physical spin model [69]. Although the microscopic exchange couplings (Jv,Jh,Jz)(J_{v},J_{h},J_{z}) are fixed, the mean-field excitation spectrum is governed by Ansatz-dependent bond parameters that set the spinon bandwidth and are not uniquely determined by the bare exchanges alone.
