More fundamentally, the unprojected Abrikosov-fermion mean-field state relaxes the single-occupancy constraint and therefore does not reside in the physical spin Hilbert space; as a consequence, its dynamical correlators do not, in general, satisfy the exact sum rules of the spin Hamiltonian, including frequency-moment sum rules that relate moments of the dynamical structure factors to equal-time correlators and exchange couplings [1, 129]. By contrast, DMRG evaluates spin correlations strictly within the physical Hilbert space, while pf-FRG incorporates self-energy and vertex renormalizations derived from the microscopic Hamiltonian [130]. For this reason, absolute energy scales, spectral weights, and detailed line shapes obtained at the mean-field level are not expected to quantitatively match those of pf-FRG or DMRG, even when expressed in units of JJ. Throughout, we therefore restrict comparisons to qualitative momentum-space features and trends, which nevertheless provide valuable insight into the symmetry properties and structure of the underlying fractionalized excitations.

VI.1 Mean-field results

Owing to SU(2) spin-rotation symmetry, it suffices to compute only the longitudinal component of the DSF

𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)=∫−∞+∞d​τ​ei​ω​τ2​π​N​∑i,jei​𝒒⋅𝒓i​j​⟨S^iz​(τ)​S^jz​(0)⟩,\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega)=\int^{+\infty}_{-\infty}\frac{d\tau\,e^{i\omega\tau}}{2\pi N}\sum_{i,j}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{ij}}\langle\hat{S}^{z}_{i}(\tau)\hat{S}^{z}_{j}(0)\rangle, (83)

where 𝒓i​j=𝒓i−𝒓j\bm{r}_{ij}=\bm{r}_{i}-\bm{r}_{j} and NN denotes the total number of sites. Inserting the Heisenberg time evolution of S^iz​(τ)=ei​H^​τ​S^iz​e−i​H^​τ\hat{S}^{z}_{i}(\tau)=e^{i\hat{H}\tau}\hat{S}^{z}_{i}e^{-i\hat{H}\tau} and expressing the spin operators in terms of fermionic spinons recasts Eq. (83) into the form

𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) =∫−∞+∞d​τ​ei​ω​τ8​π​N​∑i,jei​𝒒⋅𝒓i​j​τα​αz​τβ​βz\displaystyle=\int^{+\infty}_{-\infty}\frac{d\tau\,e^{i\omega\tau}}{8\pi N}\sum_{i,j}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{ij}}\tau^{z}_{\alpha\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\beta\beta}
×∑α,β⟨ei​H^​τ​f^i,α†​f^i,α​e−i​H^​τ​f^j,β†​f^j,β⟩.\displaystyle\times\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\langle e^{i\hat{H}\tau}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i,\alpha}e^{-i\hat{H}\tau}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{j,\beta}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\beta}\rangle. (84)

For U(1) Ansätze, given the absence of pairing terms, the spin-up and spin-down sectors decouple, allowing us to work in a basis consisting solely of annihilation operators in each spin sector, i.e., f^α†=(f^1,α†,f^2,α†,⋯,f^N,α†)\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}=(\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{1,\alpha},\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{2,\alpha},\cdots,\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{N,\alpha}). Consequently, the Hamiltonian takes the form

H^=∑α=↑,↓f^α†​ℋ^​f^α.\hat{H}=\sum_{\alpha=\uparrow,\downarrow}\hat{f}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\hat{\mathcal{H}}\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha}. (85)

We now perform a unitary transformation f^α=U​c^α\hat{f}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha}=U\hat{c}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha} such that U†​ℋ^​U=diag⁡(ϵ1,ϵ2,…,ϵN)U^{\dagger}\hat{\mathcal{H}}U=\mathrm{diag}(\epsilon_{1},\epsilon_{2},\dots,\epsilon_{N}). Substituting into Eq. (84), we obtain

𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)=∫−∞+∞d​τ​ei​ω​τ8​π​N​∑i,j,μ,μ′,ν,ν′ei​𝒒⋅𝒓i​j​τα​αz​τβ​βz​Ui,μ∗​Ui,μ′​Uj,ν∗​Uj,ν′​∑α,β⟨ei​H^​τ​c^μ,α†​c^μ′,α​e−i​H^​τ​c^ν,β†​c^ν′,β⟩.\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega)=\int^{+\infty}_{-\infty}\frac{d\tau\,e^{i\omega\tau}}{8\pi N}\sum_{i,j,\mu,\mu^{\prime},\nu,\nu^{\prime}}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{ij}}\tau^{z}_{\alpha\alpha}\tau^{z}_{\beta\beta}\,U^{*}_{i,\mu}U_{i,\mu^{\prime}}U^{*}_{j,\nu}U_{j,\nu^{\prime}}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\langle e^{i\hat{H}\tau}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mu,\alpha}\hat{c}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mu^{\prime},\alpha}e^{-i\hat{H}\tau}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\nu,\beta}\hat{c}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\nu^{\prime},\beta}\rangle. (86)

The DSF involves contributions from processes in which a fermion is annihilated in an initially occupied state (ν′,β)(\nu^{\prime},\beta) and a fermion is simultaneously created in an unoccupied state (ν,β)(\nu,\beta) at τ=0\tau=0. This particle-hole excitation persists until time τ\tau, when it is annihilated. This leads to the simplification

⟨ei​H^​τ​c^μ,α†​c^μ′,α​e−i​H^​τ​c^ν,β†​c^ν′,β⟩\displaystyle\langle e^{i\hat{H}\tau}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mu,\alpha}\hat{c}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mu^{\prime},\alpha}e^{-i\hat{H}\tau}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\nu,\beta}\hat{c}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\nu^{\prime},\beta}\rangle =e−i⁡(ϵν−ϵν′)​τ​δν′,μ​δμ′,ν​δα,β​⟨c^μ,α†​c^ν′,β⟩​⟨c^μ′,α​c^ν,β†⟩,\displaystyle=e^{-i(\epsilon_{\nu}-\epsilon_{\nu^{\prime}})\tau}\delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\nu^{\prime},\mu}\delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mu^{\prime},\nu}\delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\alpha,\beta}\langle\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\mu,\alpha}\hat{c}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\nu^{\prime},\beta}\rangle\langle\hat{c}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mu^{\prime},\alpha}\hat{c}^{\dagger}_{\nu,\beta}\rangle, (87)

which, upon substitution into Eq. (86), yields

𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) =12​N​∑i,j,μ,νei​𝒒⋅𝒓i​j​δ​(ω−ϵν+ϵμ)​Ui,μ∗​Ui,ν​Uj,ν∗​Uj,μ​nμ​(1−nν),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i,j,\mu,\nu}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{ij}}\delta(\omega-\epsilon_{\nu}+\epsilon_{\mu})U^{*}_{i,\mu}U_{i,\nu}U^{*}_{j,\nu}U_{j,\mu}n_{\mu}(1-n_{\nu}), (88)

where the fermionic occupation number is given by ni=[exp(β(ϵi−ϵF)+1]−1n_{i}=[\exp(\beta(\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{F})+1]^{-1}, with ϵF\epsilon_{F} denoting the Fermi energy.

In the zero-temperature limit, the Fermi distribution becomes a step function, and Eq. (88) simplifies to

𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) =12​N​∑i,j,μ,νei​𝒒⋅𝒓i​j​δ​(ω−ϵν+ϵμ)​Ui,μ∗​Ui,ν​Uj,ν∗​Uj,μ​Θ​(ϵF−ϵμ)​Θ​(ϵν−ϵF),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i,j,\mu,\nu}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{ij}}\delta(\omega-\epsilon_{\nu}+\epsilon_{\mu})U^{*}_{i,\mu}U_{i,\nu}U^{*}_{j,\nu}U_{j,\mu}\Theta(\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{\mu})\Theta(\epsilon_{\nu}-\epsilon_{F}), (89)

where Θ⁡(x)\Theta(x) is the Heaviside step function.

Following this calculation, Fig. 10 presents the dynamical spin structure factors (DSFs) along high-symmetry momentum paths for the same representative points as in Fig. 4. All the DSFs exhibit broad continua instead of sharp dispersive features, a hallmark of fractionalized excitations. The distribution of the dominant spectral intensity, however, varies significantly depending on the Ansatz and the specific phase under consideration, appearing at different energies and momenta across the various cases. This sensitivity of the DSF profile offers a concrete experimental handle to distinguish between competing quantum spin liquid states and provides predictions for future experiments on, e.g., the candidate trellis lattice compounds discussed in Sec. VII. It is worth mentioning that since our parton framework is strictly SU(2) spin-rotation invariant (as we do not include an antiferromagnetic order parameter), sharp modes can only appear beyond a mean-field treatment once fermion-fermion interactions are included, e.g., within the random phase approximation (RPA) that has recently been successful in accurately obtaining dynamical spin structure factors [131, 132].

We also explicitly calculate the DSF for the six specific points in the mean-field phase diagram shown in Fig. 7. For these points, the self-consistent solutions yield vanishing hopping amplitudes in certain directions, which allows for a transparent interpretation of the 𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) spectra in Fig. 12.

  • •

    Phase I: Here, χv\chi_{v} and χh\chi_{h} are vanishingly small compared to χz\chi_{z}, resulting in effectively decoupled one-dimensional zigzag chains. The spectrum is dispersionless along kyk_{y} between M′M^{\prime} and Γ′\Gamma^{\prime}. Along kxk_{x} (Γ\Gamma–M′M^{\prime}), 𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) exhibits the characteristic particle-hole continuum of a one-dimensional cosinelike band.

  • •

    Phase II: In this regime, χz\chi_{z} and χh\chi_{h} dominate while χv\chi_{v} is negligible. The triangular plaquettes carry staggered 00 and π\pi fluxes, producing alternating χh\chi_{h} hopping amplitudes. The system organizes into decoupled one-dimensional chains with uniform nearest-neighbor and alternating next-nearest-neighbor hoppings. This alternation opens a band gap, yielding a gapped 𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega). The spectrum remains dispersionless along kyk_{y}.

  • •

    Phase III: When χz\chi_{z} and χv\chi_{v} are small compared to χh\chi_{h}, the system reduces to decoupled horizontal chains with cosinelike parton dispersions. In this case, we observe a full particle-hole continuum along kxk_{x} and a dispersionless response along kyk_{y}.

  • •

    Phase IV: This π\pi-flux decoupled ladder phase arises when the hopping amplitudes along the upper and lower horizontal chains acquire opposite signs, leading to a band gap of Δ=2​χv\Delta=2\chi_{v}. The horizontal chains thus exhibit gapped cosinelike dispersions, producing a 𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) similar to phase III, but shifted by the gap. Additionally, finite dispersionless spectral weight emerges between M′M^{\prime} and Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} along kyk_{y}.

  • •

    Phase V: In this limit, horizontal and zigzag hoppings are negligible relative to vertical hopping, reducing the system to a lattice of fully decoupled dimers. The bonding-antibonding energy splitting of the dimers is 2​χv2\chi_{v}, giving rise to a finite 𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) only at ω=2​χv\omega=2\chi_{v}.

  • •

    Phase VI: With finite χz\chi_{z} and χv\chi_{v}, the system forms a two-dimensional honeycomb lattice featuring Dirac points in the band structure. Consequently, 𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega) is gapless, with dispersive features along both kxk_{x} and kyk_{y}.

Additionally, we calculate the equal-time momentum-resolved spin-spin correlation function, also known as the EQSF, which is relevant to elastic neutron scattering. This quantity can be obtained from Eq. (82) by summing the DSF over all frequencies: 𝒮z​z​(𝒒)≡∑ω𝒮z​z​(𝒒,ω),\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q})\equiv\sum_{\omega}\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q},\omega), leading to the final expression

𝒮z​z​(𝒒)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{zz}(\bm{q}) =12​N​∑i,j,μ,νei​𝒒⋅𝒓i​j​Ui,μ∗​Ui,ν​Uj,ν∗​Uj,μ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i,j,\mu,\nu}e^{i\bm{q}\cdot\bm{r}_{ij}}U^{*}_{i,\mu}U_{i,\nu}U^{*}_{j,\nu}U_{j,\mu}
×Θ⁡(ϵF−ϵμ)​Θ​(ϵν−ϵF).\displaystyle\times\Theta(\epsilon_{F}-\epsilon_{\mu})\Theta(\epsilon_{\nu}-\epsilon_{F}). (90)

The resulting EQSFs are shown in Fig. 11, evaluated at the same representative parameter points used for the dispersions in Fig. 4 and the DSF plots in Fig. 10. Once again, we observe a smooth distribution of spectral weight in the Brillouin zone and an absence of sharp Bragg peaks, as expected for quantum paramagnetic states.

VI.2 Keldysh pf-FRG analysis

To complement the mean-field results for the dynamical and equal-time spin structure factors, we employ the recently developed Keldysh extension [85, 133] of the pf-FRG [134]. The core idea of this method is to formulate a renormalization group flow for the frequency-dependent effective interactions and onsite self-energies of the Abrikosov pseudofermions, as defined in Eq. (2), by introducing a cutoff scale Λ\Lambda that suppresses low-energy dynamics. At large Λ\Lambda, the system is described by the bare microscopic Hamiltonian, while gradually lowering Λ\Lambda drives the flow toward the fully interacting regime, which is recovered at Λ=0\Lambda=0.

By utilizing the Keldysh formalism—originally developed for nonequilibrium systems—in an equilibrium setting at finite temperature TT, the method provides direct access to the real-frequency structure of the interaction vertices. This circumvents the need for an ill-conditioned analytical continuation from imaginary (Matsubara) frequencies, as would be required in conventional equilibrium formulations.

From the flowing pf-FRG vertices and self-energies, we compute both the dynamical and equal-time spin structure factors for the full spin-1/21/2 system. It is important to note that within this formalism, excitations near the Γ\Gamma point are naturally suppressed, particularly in regimes close to long-range magnetic order [133].

For the numerical calculations, we set the inverse temperature to β=1/T=10/J\beta=1/T=10/J, where J=Jz+Jh+JvJ=J_{z}+J_{h}+J_{v} defines the overall energy scale of the system. Correlations are computed up to a spatial extent of 4 lattice spacings along the 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1} direction and 2 along the 𝑻2\bm{T}_{2} direction, resulting in a total of 41 symmetry-inequivalent lattice sites. The frequency axis is discretized using a linear-logarithmic mesh comprising 43 non-negative frequencies.

All pf-FRG flows remain smooth down to Λ=0\Lambda=0, except for the ladder phase, where a kink in the flow at Λc=0.05\Lambda_{c}=0.05 signals the onset of long-range magnetic order. Accordingly, for this case, we present the spin structure factor at Λc\Lambda_{c}, while for all other cases the structure factors are shown in the fully renormalized (Λ→0\Lambda\to 0) limit.

The DSFs and EQSFs thus obtained from our analysis are arrayed in Fig. 12 for the six phases identified in the fully symmetric ternary phase diagram, alongside the corresponding mean-field results. In most cases, we find excellent qualitative agreement between the EQSFs derived from our PSG Ansätze and those obtained from the beyond-mean-field Keldysh approach.

For the DSFs, however, qualitative differences arise between the mean-field and Keldysh results. These discrepancies can be traced to two principal limitations of the Keldysh pf-FRG [133]: (1) Its inability to resolve spectral gaps when the associated order parameter is not explicitly included in the flow and (2) the absence of downward-dispersing branches toward q=0q=0 in systems with antiferromagnetic order. The first limitation is generic to FRG approaches: If an order parameter is not explicitly incorporated into the flow equations, it cannot acquire a finite value, leading in practice to gapless spectra. Implementing a general order parameter that captures spectral gaps is nontrivial, as it cannot be introduced in a system-independent manner [133]. The second limitation is more severe and stems from the systematic suppression of long-range order within pf-FRG. In this framework, transitions from the initial paramagnetic state to an ordered phase are always accompanied by a diverging susceptibility, which would necessitate a divergence in the vertex function. Since the Keldysh pf-FRG relies on avoiding divergences to fully remove cutoff dependences, one is constrained to remain in the initial paramagnetic regime, preventing the correct reproduction of long-range features. Furthermore, the fermionic decomposition of spin operators introduces additional inaccuracies, as discussed in detail in Ref. 133. Despite these caveats, the Keldysh pf-FRG remains a powerful method for resolving the dominant low-energy excitations around the ground state. This makes it particularly well suited for spin liquid candidates, where long-range order is absent and alternative approaches may fail.

Taking these limitations into account, we find that phases I and III show good agreement in terms of the principal low-energy excitations. Phases II and IV also display the expected qualitative features, aside from the absence of a spectral gap, which follows directly from limitation (1). More significant deviations from PSG-based expectations appear in phases V and VI. A comparison of the dynamical structure factors together with the equal-time spin structure factors with mean-field results suggests that (1) either beyond–mean-field corrections could account for these discrepancies, such as by incorporating fermion-fermion interactions, e.g., within an RPA framework [131, 132] or treating gauge fluctuations via Gutzwiller projection, or (2) these could be signatures of incipient magnetic orders that are captured in DMRG and Keldysh pf-FRG.

In summary, while the Keldysh pf-FRG has intrinsic limitations, it remains a valuable tool for characterizing the main low-energy excitations beyond mean-field theory, provided that the above constraints are properly considered.

VI.3 DMRG calculations

Another unbiased approach for the calculation of spin correlation functions is DMRG [135, 136, 137]. Unlike Keldysh pf-FRG computations, which operate at small but finite temperatures, DMRG directly accesses the zero-temperature ground-state properties of the system.

Our DMRG calculations are, in practice, based on the variational optimization of a matrix product state (MPS) wave function. Once such an MPS representation of the ground state is obtained for a given set of Hamiltonian parameters, the spin correlation functions can be readily computed. DMRG is particularly powerful for one-dimensional systems, for which it is known to provide extremely accurate results. In our context, this is advantageous for certain phases (e.g., I, III, and IV in the mean-field phase diagram of Fig. 7), which become effectively quasi-one-dimensional due to the reduced couplings along some directions (refer to Table 6).

Here, we simulate the trellis lattice system on a cylindrical geometry with open boundary conditions along 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1} and periodic boundary conditions along the 𝑻2\bm{T}_{2} direction22 2 Fully periodic boundaries would require a quadratic increase in the number of states needed for the same accuracy, making the computation prohibitively expensive.. A well-known limitation of two-dimensional DMRG is that the number of states required grows exponentially with the system width [137], which restricts accessible system sizes. In this work, we consider a 10×510\times 5 system (i.e., with up to 10 sites in the periodic direction), with a maximum MPS bond dimension of 24002400. Our sweeping strategy involves starting with many sweeps at relatively small bond dimensions and gradually increasing the bond dimension until convergence is achieved. Convergence is defined as the point where the truncation error falls below 10−510^{-5}, which is typically satisfied after 𝒪⁡(102)\mathcal{O}(10^{2}) sweeps. To facilitate the buildup of long-range correlations, we also add a small noise term to the density matrix during the early sweeps, which is subsequently turned off [138].

The resulting equal-time structure factors, shown in the rightmost column of Fig. 12, display excellent agreement with the Keldysh pf-FRG results across all six phases (I–VI). In particular, the DMRG calculations capture features that lie beyond mean-field theory, which are also visible in the pf-FRG spectra, albeit broadened due to the finite temperatures intrinsic to the latter formalism.

VII Material realizations

The rich physics of magnetic frustration on the trellis lattice that we have discussed so far can also, in principle, be explored in solid-state materials. To this end, we introduce four compounds—SrCu2​O3\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, CaCu2​O3\text{CaCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, MgV2​O5\text{MgV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}}, and CaV2​O5\text{CaV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}}—that are known to realize the trellis lattice geometry. Both Cu2+ and V4+ ions carry spin-1/21/2. To avoid confusion, we label the exchange couplings in order of strictly increasing distances between magnetic sites. In the various realizations of the trellis lattice, the three main couplings—namely, the chain (JhJ_{h}), rung (JvJ_{v}), and sawtooth (JzJ_{z}) interactions—are realized through different intersite distances depending on the compound. In Fig. 13, the colors purple, light blue, and blue are used to denote JhJ_{h}, JvJ_{v}, and JzJ_{z}, respectively.

VII.1 Density functional theory

For the four materials, we apply a DFT-based energy-mapping approach that has been successfully used to understand many low-dimensional copper-based quantum magnets [139, 140, 141]. Our approach employs all electron electronic structure calculations using the full potential local orbital basis set [142] with a generalized gradient approximation exchange correlation potential [143]. Strong electronic correlations on Cu2+ and V4+ 3​d3d orbitals are treated with a DFT+UU correction [144]. This correction has two parameters, the on-site interaction UU and the Hund’s coupling JHJ_{\rm H}. As the latter is not expected to be strongly material dependent, we fix it to be JH=1J_{\rm H}=1 eV for Cu [145] and JH=0.68J_{\rm H}=0.68 eV for V [146]. The interaction strength UU determines the energy scale of the magnetic interactions and is taken from experimental Curie-Weiss temperatures whenever possible. For the energy mapping, we classify all spin configurations in low-symmetry supercell structures and map large sets of DFT+UU total energies to the Heisenberg Hamiltonian written as ℋ^=∑i<jJi​j​𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j\hat{\mathcal{H}}=\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}, where every bond is counted only once. Rather than making assumptions about an important subset of exchange couplings, we calculate between 9 and 12 interactions for each of the four materials, and the result flags the important couplings in an unbiased fashion; in most cases, we also gather information about exchange paths coupling the trellis layers, which are important for possible magnetic orders.

SrCu2​O3\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} is a cuprate compound exhibiting a flat trellis lattice [Fig. 13(b)], with couplings identified as Jh≡J4J_{h}\equiv J_{4}, Jv≡J3J_{v}\equiv J_{3}, and Jz≡J1J_{z}\equiv J_{1}. We perform our calculations using the T=100T=100 K structure with C​m​m​mCmmm space group, as determined by single-crystal x-ray diffraction [147]. The DFT energy mapping reveals a system composed of robust two-leg JhJ_{h}-JvJ_{v} ladders, with Jh≈2​JvJ_{h}\approx 2J_{v}. The zigzag coupling JzJ_{z} is found to be weaker and ferromagnetic. Reported spin gap values include Δ=420\Delta=420 K based on susceptibility data [57], and Δ=680\Delta=680 K from Cu NMR [148]. The susceptibility presented in Ref. 57 is challenging to interpret via a traditional Curie-Weiss fit, as χ−1\chi^{-1} exhibits a negative slope at high temperatures. Using the refined Curie-Weiss fitting procedure from Ref. 149, we obtain θCW=−626\theta_{\rm CW}=-626 K; however, this result is unreliable due to the limited temperature range (data only extend to 650 K). Efforts to determine accurate Hamiltonian parameters have employed simplified models, such as the two-leg ladder approximation [150, 151, 152]. Among the computed Hamiltonians, the one obtained with U=8.5U=8.5 eV appears most consistent with the expectation that JhJ_{h} should be approximately twice the spin gap, i.e., around 1400 K. The extracted values are Jh=J4=1656​(14)J_{h}=J_{4}=1656(14) K, Jv=J3=945​(16)J_{v}=J_{3}=945(16) K, and JzJ_{z} == J1J_{1} == −289​(27)-289(27) K. Besides the three trellis lattice couplings, we obtain the diagonal coupling in the ladder J8=48​(14)J_{8}=48(14) K as well as interlayer couplings J2=41​(22)J_{2}=41(22) K, J5=−9​(23)J_{5}=-9(23) K, J6=14​(9)J_{6}=14(9) K and J7=−17​(13)J_{7}=-17(13) K that are small compared to the dominant interaction. For the rung-to-chain ratio Jv/JhJ_{v}/J_{h}, we have Jv/Jh=0.57J_{v}/J_{h}=0.57, which compares well to the value Jv/Jh=0.5J_{v}/J_{h}=0.5 favored by Johnston [152] after weighing various experimental facts. Our result can be compared with an early ab initio study [153] that reports Jh=1870J_{h}=1870 K, Jv=1670J_{v}=1670 K, J1=−145J_{1}=-145 K and thus a rather large rung-to-chain ratio of Jv/Jh=0.89J_{v}/J_{h}=0.89. On the other hand, our results are in good agreement with local density approximation+U (LDA+U) calculations reported in Ref. 50 yielding Jh=1795J_{h}=1795 K, Jv=809J_{v}=809 K, J1=−200J_{1}=-200 K.

CaCu2​O3\text{CaCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} exhibits a buckled trellis lattice [Fig. 13(d)]. We use the T=10T=10 K structure with P​n​m​aPnma space group obtained via neutron diffraction [156]. Here, the exchange couplings are given by Jh≡J5J_{h}\equiv J_{5}, Jv≡J2J_{v}\equiv J_{2}, and Jz≡J1J_{z}\equiv J_{1}. Energy mapping shows that the antiferromagnetic chain coupling JhJ_{h} dominates over the other two. Using the Curie-Weiss fitting method of Ref. 149 to fit the susceptibility from Ref. 156 [see Fig. 13(c)], we find θCW=−796\theta_{\rm CW}=-796 K. In contrast, a conventional χ−1\chi^{-1} fit misleadingly suggests θCW≈0\theta_{\rm CW}\approx 0, inconsistent with the estimated spin chain scale Jh≡J∥=2000​(300)J_{h}\equiv J_{\parallel}=2000(300) K [156]. These results are consistent with the previous estimate of J∥J_{\parallel} within error bars. An inelastic neutron scattering study by Lake et al. [154] determined Jh=1880J_{h}=1880 K, supporting earlier quantum chemistry predictions [157, 158] that JvJ_{v} is significantly smaller than JhJ_{h}. To account for the incommensurate magnetic order observed at TN=25T_{\rm N}=25 K [156], interlayer couplings would be important, but in the present study, at J3J_{3} == −7​(9)-7(9) K, J4=−6​(17)J_{4}=-6(17) K, and J6=−12​(9)J_{6}=-12(9) K, we have not been able to suppress the error bars sufficiently.

MgV2​O5\text{MgV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}} is another material that realizes a buckled trellis lattice. Our calculations are based on the T=83T=83 K powder x-ray diffraction structure with C​m​c​mCmcm space group [159]. In this case, the relevant couplings are Jh≡J3J_{h}\equiv J_{3}, Jv≡J2J_{v}\equiv J_{2}, and Jz≡J1J_{z}\equiv J_{1} [Fig. 13(f)]. DFT energy mapping indicates a two-leg ladder model, with the rung coupling JvJ_{v} being comparable in strength to the chain coupling JhJ_{h}, and with the sawtooth coupling JzJ_{z} being ferromagnetic. The Curie-Weiss temperature has been reported as θCW=−174\theta_{\rm CW}=-174 K, although this value is sensitive to the choice of the constant van-Vleck contribution χ0\chi_{0}. Varying χ0\chi_{0} between 0 and 0.7×10−50.7\times 10^{-5} emu/mol yields θCW\theta_{\rm CW} values ranging from −205-205 K to −77-77 K, with all χ−1\chi^{-1} fits appearing equally satisfactory. Since onsite Coulomb interaction values much below U=2.5U=2.5 eV are difficult to justify for V4+, we consider the U=3U=3 eV set of couplings: JhJ_{h} == J3J_{3} == 147​(1)147(1) K, JvJ_{v} == J2J_{2} == 100​(1)100(1) K, and JzJ_{z} == J1J_{1} == −44​(1)-44(1) K (corresponding to θCW=−83\theta_{\rm CW}=-83 K and a rung-to-chain ratio Jv/Jh=0.68J_{v}/J_{h}=0.68). Alternatively, for U=2.5U=2.5 eV, we find Jh=J3=151​(1)J_{h}=J_{3}=151(1) K, Jv=J2=108​(1)J_{v}=J_{2}=108(1) K, and Jz=J1=−37​(1)J_{z}=J_{1}=-37(1) K, with θCW=−94\theta_{\rm CW}=-94 K and Jv/Jh=0.72J_{v}/J_{h}=0.72. A perturbation-theory estimate of the couplings based on LDA+U within the linear muffin-tin orbital basis [62, 63] reported Jh=144J_{h}=144 K, Jv=92J_{v}=92 K, Jz=60J_{z}=60 K which is very similar for the ladder but has a different sign for the zigzag coupling.

The fourth compound that we analyze is CaV2​O5\text{CaV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}}, which also realizes a buckled trellis lattice. We base our calculations on the room-temperature x-ray powder diffraction structure with P​m​m​nPmmn space group [160] [Fig. 13(h)]. Here, the relevant couplings are Jh≡J3J_{h}\equiv J_{3}, Jv≡J2J_{v}\equiv J_{2}, and Jz≡J1J_{z}\equiv J_{1}. Fitting the susceptibility data from Ref. 160 using the Curie-Weiss approach of Ref. 149 [Fig. 13(g)], we obtain θCW=−258\theta_{\rm CW}=-258 K. This result suggests, similarly to MgV2​O5\text{MgV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}}, that a relatively small UU is appropriate for this compound. This places CaV2​O5\text{CaV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}} in the regime of a two-leg ladder with very strong rungs, characterized by Jv/Jh=4.5J_{v}/J_{h}=4.5, consistent with the scenario proposed by Millet et al. A QMC study [51] arrived at a set of interactions Jh=135J_{h}=135 K, Jv=665J_{v}=665 K, and Jz=−25J_{z}=-25 K which is quite close to our ab initio result. As far as subleading couplings are concerned, the diagonals in the ladder J6=18​(4)J_{6}=18(4) K are the most important, and interlayer couplings such as J4=1​(2)J_{4}=1(2) K and J7=4​(2)J_{7}=4(2) K are below 1% of the dominant interaction. This makes CaV2​O5\text{CaV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}} a good approximation of a two-dimensional material.

VII.2 Keldysh pf-FRG

In this section, we employ the Keldysh formalism combined with the DFT-derived couplings to analyze the materials discussed above.

We begin with CaCu2​O3\text{CaCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, which—due to its weak interchain couplings J2≡JzJ_{2}\equiv J_{z} and J3≡JvJ_{3}\equiv J_{v}—is close to being a one-dimensional material. This interpretation is supported by the equal-time spin structure factor in Fig. 14, which exhibits nearly uniform behavior along qyq_{y}. Consequently, the system effectively realizes one-dimensional chains along 𝑻1\bm{T}_{1}. The cyclic exchange JcyclJ_{\text{cycl}} [164] cannot be modeled here, as it requires quartic spin interactions that lie beyond the truncation of the FRG. While this four-spin term frustrates the spin chains, its strength in CaCu2​O3\text{CaCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}} is relatively weak (Jcycl=4J_{\text{cycl}}=4 meV [154]) compared to the approximate threshold Jcycl/J1≈0.25J_{\text{cycl}}/J_{1}\approx 0.25 for disrupting binding [164], implying that neglecting it should introduce only minor discrepancies. The dynamical spin structure factor in Fig. 14(b) qualitatively matches the experiment results [154]. The absence of the q=0q=0 branch, a limitation of the Keldysh formalism, is not critical, since this feature is typically unresolved experimentally as well. Up to an expected mismatch in the frequency scale—intrinsic to qualitative methods such as pf-FRG—our description is broadly consistent with the data.

To further test this agreement, we investigate the measured difference between strongly and weakly coupled regimes of the spin chains. Strong coupling produces a modulation along the interchain direction at 1/Qrung1/Q_{\text{rung}}, which should vanish in the weak-coupling case. Lake et al. [154] introduced integrated frequency slices to quantify deviations from the expected (1+cos⁡(Qrung))​χb+(1−cos⁡(Qrung))​χa​b(1+\cos(Q_{\text{rung}}))\chi_{b}+(1-\cos(Q_{\text{rung}}))\chi_{ab} form, dominated experimentally by the anti-bonding susceptibility χa​b\chi_{ab}. Since we cannot disentangle bonding (χb\chi_{b}) and anti-bonding (χa​b\chi_{ab}) susceptibilities directly, we interpret the full excitation spectrum instead. Figure 14(c) shows the integrated dynamical susceptibility,

Δ​S​(ωl)=∫ωlωu[S⁡(ω,qh,max)−S⁡(ω,qh,min)]​𝑑ω,\displaystyle\Delta S(\omega_{l})=\int_{\omega_{l}}^{\omega_{u}}\Big[S(\omega,q_{h,\text{max}})-S(\omega,q_{h,\text{min}})\Big]\,\mathrm{d}\omega, (91)

with a constant offset removed. Here, we use qh,max=(π,π/drung)Tq_{h,\text{max}}=(\pi,\pi/d_{\text{rung}})^{T}, qh,min=(π,0)Tq_{h,\text{min}}=(\pi,0)^{T}, and ωu=5​J\omega_{u}=5J sets the upper frequency cutoff. This choice captures the essential modulation falloff without relying on arbitrary frequency windows. The correlations decay rapidly to zero around ω≈0.27\omega\approx 0.27, followed by a sign reversal at larger ω/J\omega/J, indicating that χb\chi_{b} eventually dominates over χa​b\chi_{ab}. We interpret this as a remnant of strong chain interactions persisting at higher frequencies, with a small amplitude, potentially enhancing the singlet channel. Nevertheless, the Keldysh pf-FRG is, in principle, capable of capturing triplons that induce χb\chi_{b}-dominated modulation at low frequencies, extending beyond mean-field analyses.

For the remaining trellis lattice materials, no experimental benchmarks for the dynamical spin structure factor 𝒮⁡(𝒒,ω)\mathcal{S}(\bm{q},\omega) yet exist. We therefore use the Keldysh pf-FRG calculations to make predictions. As discussed in Ref. 133, it should be kept in mind that potential gaps and exponentially suppressed branches at q=0q=0 are not resolved, restricting our predictions to the low-energy sector.

For SrCu2​O3\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, the strongest couplings are again along the chains, but significant interchain couplings convert the system into coupled two-leg ladders [165]. This is reflected in the equal-time spin structure factor shown in Fig. 15(a), which exhibits two distinct maxima along qyq_{y}, consistent with phase IV in Fig. 12. The experimentally known gap of Egap∼36E_{\text{gap}}\sim 36 meV [57] lies far below the Keldysh resolution (Egap/J≈0.015E_{\text{gap}}/J\approx 0.015). Moreover, doping rapidly introduces in-gap states and suppresses singlet-triplet excitations [166]. We therefore consider the influence of the gap to be small and expect the remaining excitation features to be well captured by the Keldysh pf-FRG. The dynamical spin structure factor Fig. 15(b) closely resembles that of the rung-ladder phase (phase IV in Fig. 7). Its mean-field counterpart corresponds to a quadratic hopping Hamiltonian with π\pi-flux per square plaquette, obtained as a saddle point of the parent U(1) Ansätze U2, U3, and U6 in Fig. 3.

It is worth noting that the Keldysh FRG flow does not monotonically continue to vanishing cutoff scales. Instead, as shown in Fig. 15(c), the imaginary part of the susceptibility begins to grow precisely at the position of the kink, which we regard as a signal to terminate the flow, since it should vanish by symmetry. In the pf-FRG framework, such a breakdown serve as an indicator for the onset of magnetic ordering: The FRG cannot flow into a symmetry-broken phase and therefore, the susceptibility diverges at the corresponding phase boundary [134, 167]. This behavior can also occur in the vicinity of symmetry-broken phases—even though a purely two-dimensional model should not order at finite temperature as dictated by the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem—which is why we observe these ordering tendencies. Compared to strongly ordered systems, however, the kink seen here is relatively small. This interpretation is supported by the fact that raising the temperature removes the kink entirely, allowing the flow to proceed down to Λ=0\Lambda=0. Given that the cutoff at the divergence is already small, we use the β=0.1​J\beta=0.1J data above the nonmonotonicity for the equal-time and dynamic spin structure factors, thereby capturing both the incipient ordering tendencies and the underlying spin liquid behavior, which lie beyond the scope of a pure mean-field analysis.

For CaV2​O5\text{CaV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}}, DFT results identify a two-legged ladder, similar to SrCu2​O3\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, but with significantly stronger rung couplings (Jv/Jh=4.5J_{v}/J_{h}=4.5). Accordingly, the equal-time spin structure factor [Fig. 16(a)] shows dominant modulation along qyq_{y}, consistent with the ladder-dimer phase V in Fig. 7. The dynamical spin structure factor [Fig. 16(b)] shares similarities with that of SrCu2​O3\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}, though the spectral weight is more broadly distributed beyond ω=0\omega=0. This broadening stems from the higher breakdown scale Λ≈0.08\Lambda\approx 0.08, about twice that of SrCu2​O3\text{SrCu}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{3}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{3}}\text{}}. While there is no direct correspondence between the cutoff and a transition temperature or an energy scale [134], a larger divergence scale qualitatively reflects stronger ordering tendencies. Consequently, this finite cutoff still manifests in the dynamical spin structure factor and leads to an exponential broadening of all ω≠0\omega\neq 0 excitations, unrelated to any intrinsic signatures of spin liquid behavior.

Finally, for MgV2​O5\text{MgV}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{2}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{2}}\text{}}\text{O}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\vphantom{\text{2}}\smash[t]{\text{5}}}^{\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\hphantom{\text{5}}\text{}}, we consider two viable DFT configurations, with UU == 33 eV and UU == 2.52.5 eV. Both exhibit strong ordering tendencies within pf-FRG that persist even at elevated temperatures. We therefore refrain from presenting the dynamical spin structure factor, as ordering effects and the cutoff-related broadening reduce the applicability of the Keldysh pf-FRG beyond the typical ground-state analysis known from standard Matsubara pf-FRG (and the pseudo-Majorana functional renormalization group). The corresponding equal-time spin structure factors [Figs. 16(c) and  16(d)] appear nearly identical, suggesting similar ground-state properties. However, the flow analysis reveals that the imaginary part of susceptibility, signifying the symmetry-breaking tendency, grows 30 times larger for U=2.5U=2.5 eV than for U=3U=3 eV, indicating a stronger ordering propensity. In both cases, the systems appear magnetically ordered, and further analysis should therefore employ methods such as linear spin-wave theory, which are suited for dynamic correlations on top of magnetically ordered states.

VIII Discussion and outlook

Our work introduces a unique class of QSLs, namely, semi-Dirac spin liquids. The fermionic parton constructions presented here provide a foundation for studying the role of U(1) gauge fluctuations beyond the mean-field approximation. For conventional Dirac spin liquids, the impact of gauge fluctuations has been extensively analyzed, particularly on triangular and kagome lattices, where such states are regarded as excellent variational candidates for the ground state of the spin-1/21/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet [113, 4, 5]. In these systems, gauge fluctuations significantly modify spectroscopic signatures [168, 169, 170, 171], while preserving the gapless nature of excitations [172, 6, 5, 173, 174] and their disordered character without lattice or spin-rotation symmetry breaking [175, 176]. Moreover, singlet and triplet monopoles remain gapless on kagome and triangular lattices, without destabilizing the U(1) Dirac state [177, 178]. By contrast, the influence of gauge fluctuations on U(1) semi-Dirac states with neutral fermions remains unexplored, in constrast to effects of Coulomb interactions on charged fermions [179]. It is therefore important to investigate how Gutzwiller projection modifies the long-distance behavior of spin-spin correlations and the spin structure factor. Possible outcomes include renormalization of the mean-field exponents, as occurs in Dirac spin liquids [113, 180, 181], or more drastic effects such as gap opening [128] or spontaneous symmetry breaking [182]. Since, Gutzwiller projection incorporates spinon interactions in a nonperturbative manner, substantial modifications of low-energy dynamical structure factors are likely. A complementary direction is the symmetry analysis of singlet and triplet monopoles and their condensation patterns into valence-bond crystal and magnetic orders, respectively, which would yield crucial insights into the spectroscopic fingerprints of low-energy monopole excitations [183]. Constructing variational wave functions for monopole excitations and estimating their scaling dimensions would provide further guidance on their stability. Another interesting avenue would be to identify the key ingredients necessary to construct tight-binding models that yield generalized semi-Dirac dispersions, i.e., where the leading term is ∝|𝐤|2​N\propto|\mathbf{k}|^{2N} (with N>1N>1) or host type-II semi-Dirac fermions wherein the spinons disperse with a combination of different momentum components away from the reciprocal lattice vectors [184].

While not stabilized for the nearest-neighbor Heisenberg model on the trellis lattice, the semi-Dirac spin liquid represents a distinct symmetry-allowed quantum spin liquid, motivating the search for microscopic spin models in which it may emerge as a viable variational ground state. At the mean-field level, these states appear only at fine-tuned phase boundaries, and it remains to be seen whether upon inclusion of quantum fluctuations the sDSL is robust against its many potential instabilities such as monopole proliferation and confinement, Higgsing of the U(1) gauge boson to ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, or spontaneous symmetry breaking driven by (strong) fermion interactions [96]. In the scenario that the sDSL happens to be stable to these perturbations and is realized as a phase while being the variational ground state over a region of parameter space of the nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic model, it would be interesting to identify additional interactions that could potentially enhance its region of stability. These include terms such as ring-exchange, XXZ anisotropy, etc., and to this effect, it would be important to map out the corresponding ground state phase diagrams using state-of-the-art many-body methods, including variational Monte Carlo, DMRG, and tensor-network approaches. It is also valuable to systematically determine which lattice and Hamiltonian symmetries are required to host semi-Dirac spectra [185, 186, 187], and to examine their feasibility across other wallpaper groups and in three-dimensional lattices. A particularly intriguing direction is the realization of semi-Dirac QSLs in tight-binding models on two-dimensional hyperbolic lattices [188, 189, 190, 191], a setting that remains largely unexplored.

Given the delicate competition between quantum spin liquid and weak magnetic order in the spin-1/21/2 nearest-neighbor Heisenberg antiferromagnet, it would be instructive to study this interplay using variational Monte Carlo. Jastrow-Slater wave functions have previously provided accurate estimates of order parameters and phase boundaries in frustrated magnets. Should the magnetic order parameter vanish in the thermodynamic limit, the U(1) and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} states classified here would constitute strong candidates for the true ground state. Comparing the variational energies of their Gutzwiller-projected wave functions would then allow one to identify the lowest-energy phase and thereby elucidate the microscopic nature of the ground state. In particular, the quantum melting of classical incommensurate spirals has been argued to give rise to gapped ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} QSLs [192, 193], providing a concrete starting point for future investigations.

Finally, we note that recent advances in quantum simulation have enabled the realization of tunable Heisenberg and XXZ models on arbitrary lattice geometries, including the trellis lattice [194, 195]. Such synthetic quantum systems offer yet another pathway to probe the correlated phases discussed in this work, complementing solid-state materials. In particular, these platforms’ capability for site-resolved measurements provides direct microscopic access to quantities that are typically inaccessible in bulk experiments [196]. This includes not only local spin correlations but also more refined probes such as the entanglement entropy [197, 198], thereby offering unique insights into the underlying quantum many-body physics.

[1−(−1)wC2]​θ=0,{θ∈[0,2​π)if ​wC2=0,θ=0,πif ​wC2=1.\displaystyle\big[1-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\big]\theta=0,\quad\begin{cases}\theta\in[0,2\pi)&\text{if }w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0,\\ \theta=0,\pi&\text{if }w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1.\end{cases} (122)

Substituting back into Eq. (120), we find that the general solution is

ϕC2​(x,y,u)=−(−1)wC2​(x​θC2​T1+y​θC2​T2)+ρC2,u,\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}(x\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}+y\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}})+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (123)

where ρC2,u≡ϕC2​(0,0,u)\rho_{C_{2},u}\equiv\phi_{C_{2}}(0,0,u).

We now consider the PSG associated with σx\sigma_{x}. Using Eqs. (95) and (96) together with Eq. (118), we obtain

Δ1​ϕσx​(x,y,u)=−(−1)wσx​θσx​T1+y​θ​(1+(−1)wσx),\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}}}(x,y,u)=-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}}+y\theta\big(1+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\big),
Δ2​ϕσx​(x,y,u)=−(−1)wσx​θσx​T2+(−1)wσx​(y−1)​θ,\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}(y-1)\theta\,, (124)

which must satisfy the consistency relation analogous to Eq. (121),

Δi​ϕσx​(x,y,u)+Δi+1​ϕσx​(x−1,y,u)\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)+\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+1}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x-1,y,u)
=Δi+1​ϕσx​(x,y,u)+Δi​ϕσx​(x,y−1,u).\displaystyle=\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+1}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)+\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y-1,u)\,. (125)

For i=1,2i=1,2 in Eq. (125), substituting Eq. (124) imposes the following constraints:

[1+(−1)wσx]​θ=0,{θ=0,πif ​wσx=0,θ∈[0,2​π)if ​wσx=1.\displaystyle\left[1+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\right]\theta=0,\quad\begin{cases}\theta=0,\pi&\text{if }w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0,\\ \theta\in[0,2\pi)&\text{if }w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1\,.\end{cases} (126)

Combining these constraints with Eq. (124), the general solution for ϕσx​(x,y,u)\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) is

ϕσx​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) =−(−1)wσx​[x​θσx​T1+y​θσx​T2]\displaystyle=-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\big[x\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}}+y\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}}\big]
+(−1)wσx​12​y​(y−1)​θ+ρσx,u,\displaystyle\quad+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\frac{1}{2}y(y-1)\theta+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}\,, (127)

where ρσx,u=ϕσx​(0,0,u)\rho_{\sigma_{x},u}=\phi_{{\sigma_{x}}}(0,0,u). To summarize, the constraints obtained from Eqs. (122) and (126) are compiled in Table 7.

Continuing with our derivation, substituting Eq. (123) into Eq. (98) yields the conditions

ρC2,u+(−1)wC2​ρC2,u¯=θC2\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{C_{2}},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}
wC2=1:θC2​Ti=0,π.\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1:\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{C_{2}T_{i}}}=0,\pi\,. (128)

Similarly, substituting the solution (127) into Eq. (99) leads to

wσx=0:θσx​T1=θ,ρσx,u+ρσx,u¯=θσx,\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0:\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}=\theta,\quad\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}}}, (129)
wσx=1:θσx​T1=2​θσx​T2+θ,ρσx,u−ρσx,u¯=θσx.\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1:\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}=2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+\theta,\quad\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}}}\,. (130)

Furthermore, one can use Eq. (100) to obtain

ρσx,u−ρσx,u=θ1+(−1)wσx​[θσx​T1−θ],\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}[\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}-\theta]\,, (131)

while Eq. (101) leads to the following constraints depending on the different choices of (wC2,wσx)(w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}},w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}):

(i) wC2=0,wσx=0:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0\;:
2​θC2​T2+θσx​T1=2​θσx​T2+θC2​T1,\displaystyle 2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{C_{2}T_{2}}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}=2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}, (132)
ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯+ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯=θ2−θσx​T12.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}-\frac{\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}}{2}.
(ii) wC2=1,wσx=0:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0\;:
θC2​T1=θσx​T1,\displaystyle\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}, (133)
ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯−ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯=θ2−θσx​T2−θC2​T2.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}.
(iii) wC2=0,wσx=1:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1\;:
θC2​T1=−θσx​T1,\displaystyle\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}=-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}, (134)
ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯−ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯=θ2−θσx​T2−θC2​T2.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}.
(iv) wC2=1,wσx=1:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1\;:
θσx​T1+θC2​T1=2​(θσx​T2+θC2​T2),\displaystyle\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}=2(\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}), (135)
ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯+ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯=θ2−θσx​T12.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}-\frac{\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}}{2}.

Finally, we are left with the constraint (97), which yields the following conditions:

(i) wC2=0,wσx=0:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0\;:
2​θσx​T2+θC2​T1=2​θC2​T2+θσx​T1,\displaystyle 2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}=2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}},
ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯+ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯=θC2​σx.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}. (136)
(ii) wC2=1,wσx=0:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0\;:

ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯−ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯=θC2​σx.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}. (137)
(iii) wC2=0,wσx=1:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1\;:
θC2​T1=−θσx​T1,\displaystyle\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}=-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}},
ρC2,u+ρσx,u¯−ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯=θC2​σx.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}. (138)
(iv) wC2=1,wσx=1:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1\;:
2​(θC2​T2+θσx​T2)=θσx​T1+θC2​T1,\displaystyle 2(\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}})=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}},
ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯+ρC2,u−ρσx,u¯=θC2​σx.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}. (139)

It is worth emphasizing that all the abovementioned U(1) phases may not be gauge independent. Some of them can be fixed using a local gauge transformation of the form

W⁡(x,y,u)=ℱz​(x​θx+y​θy).W(x,y,u)=\mathcal{F}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(x\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}+y\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}). (140)

This transformation does not alter the structure of the translational gauges, except for introducing global phases. These global phases do not affect the Ansatz and are therefore irrelevant. The gauge transformations for C2C^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2} and σx\sigma^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x} are now given by

ϕ~C2\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}} =x⁡[−θx−(−1)wC2​θC2​T1−(−1)wC2​θx]+y⁡[−θy−(−1)wC2​θC2​T2−(−1)wC2​θy]+ρC2,u\displaystyle=x[-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{C_{2}T_{1}}}-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}]+y[-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{C_{2}T_{2}}}-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}]+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u} (141)
ϕ~σx\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}} =x[−θx−(−1)wσxθσx​T1+(−1)wσxθx]+y[−θy−(−1)wσxθσx​T2+(−1)wσxθx−(−1)wσxθy\displaystyle=x[-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}]+y[-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}
+12(−1)wσx(y−1)θ]+ρσx,u.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}(y-1)\theta]+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}\,. (142)

In the following, we provide the details of the gauge fixing for the four distinct cases of (wC2,wσx)(w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}},w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}) using the gauge-transformed solutions obtained above.

  1. (i)

    wC2=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0, wσx=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0:
    Choosing 2​θx=−θC2​T12\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}=-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}} and 2​θy=−θC2​T22\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}=-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}} in Eq. (129) yields

    ϕ~C2​(x,y,u)=ρC2,u,\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (143)
    ϕ~σx​(x,y,u)=−x​θσx​T1−y​θσx​T2+12​y​(y−1)​θ+ρσx,u.\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=-x\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}-y\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+\tfrac{1}{2}y(y-1)\theta+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}\,. (144)
  2. (ii)

    wC2=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1, wσx=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0:
    Here, selecting θx−2​θy=θσx​T2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}-2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}} sets θσx​T2=0\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}=0. From Eqs. (128), (129), and  (133) we obtain θC2​T1=θσx​T1=θ=n​π\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}=\theta=n\pi and θC2​T2=nC2​T2​π\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}=n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}\pi. Thus,

    ϕ~C2​(x,y,u)=x​θC2​T1+y​θC2​T2+ρC2,u,\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=x\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}+y\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (145)
    ϕ~σx​(x,y,u)=−x​θσx​T1+12​y​(y−1)​θ+ρσx,u.\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=-x\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}+\tfrac{1}{2}y(y-1)\theta+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}\,. (146)
  3. (iii)

    wC2=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0, wσx=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1:
    Upon choosing 2​θx=−θC2​T12\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}=-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}} and 2​θy=−θC2​T22\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}=-\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}, and using  (130) and Eqs. (134) , we find

    ϕ~C2​(x,y,u)=ρC2,u,\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (147)
    ϕ~σx​(x,y,u)=y​θσx​T2−12​y​(y−1)​θ+ρσx,u.\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=y\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}-\tfrac{1}{2}y(y-1)\theta+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}\,. (148)
  4. (iv)

    wC2=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1, wσx=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1:
    From Eqs. (128), (130), and (135), we have θC2​Ti=nC2​Ti​π\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{i}}=n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{i}}\pi, θσx​T1=2​θσx​T2+θ\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}=2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+\theta, and θσx​T1+θC2​T1=2​(θσx​T2+θC2​T2)\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}=2(\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}). The choice θx=θσx​T2\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}} gives

    ϕ~C2​(x,y,u)=θC2​T1​x+θC2​T2​y+ρC2,u,\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}x+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}y+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (149)
    ϕ~σx​(x,y,u)=θC2​T1​x−12​y​(y−1)​θ+ρσx,u.\displaystyle\tilde{\phi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}x-\tfrac{1}{2}y(y-1)\theta+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}\,. (150)

To fix the parameters ρ…\rho_{\ldots} for all relevant symmetry operations, i.e., σx\sigma_{x} and C2C_{2}, we apply a gauge transformation W⁡(r,u)=ℱz​(ϕu)W(r,u)=\mathcal{F}_{z}(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{u}) that depends only on the sublattice index uu. This yields

ρ~C2,u=−ϕu+ρC2,u+(−1)wC2​ϕu¯,\displaystyle\tilde{\rho}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=-\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bar{u}}, (151)
ρ~σx,u=−ϕu+ρσx,u+(−1)wσx​ϕu¯.\displaystyle\tilde{\rho}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=-\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{u}+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bar{u}}\,. (152)

From the cyclic relations (98) and (99), we obtain

ρC2,u+(−1)wC2​ρC2,u¯=θC2,\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}, (153)
ρσx,u+(−1)wσx​ρσx,u¯=θσx.\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}. (154)

Using Eq. (97), we also find

ρC2,u\displaystyle\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u} +(−1)wC2​ρσx,u¯\displaystyle+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}} (155)
+(−1)wC2+wσx​ρC2,u+(−1)wσx​ρσx,u¯=θC2​σx.\displaystyle+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}+w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}.

These conditions allow us to fix the ρ\rho parameters for the four cases of (wC2,wσx)(w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}},w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}):

  1. (i)

    wC2=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0, wσx=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0:
    Choosing ϕ2=ϕ1−ρC2,1+θC2/2\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}=\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}-\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},1}+\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}/2 and combining with Eq. (153) yields ρ~C2,u=θC2/2\tilde{\rho}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}/2. Using the IGG freedom to eliminate any global phase, we fix ρC2,u=0{\rho}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=0. From Eq. (155), we find 2​ρσx,u=θC2​σx2\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}, which after fixing a global phase gives ρσx,u={0,nσx​π}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=\{0,n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\pi\}.

  2. (ii)

    wC2=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=0, wσx=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1:
    As in the previous case, we can set ρ~C2,u=0\tilde{\rho}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=0. Equation (154) then gives ρσx,2=ρσx,1+nσx​π\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},2}=\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},1}+n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\pi. Using the IGG freedom to set ρσx,1=0\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},1}=0, we obtain ρσx,u={0,nσx​π}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=\{0,n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\pi\}.

  3. (iii)

    wC2=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1, wσx=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=0:
    Choosing ϕ1+ϕ2=ρC2,1\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}+\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}=\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},1} sets ρ~C2,1=0\tilde{\rho}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},1}=0. From Eq. (153), we then obtain ρC2,u={0,nC2​π}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=\{0,n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}\pi\}. Similarly, Eq. (154) gives ρσx,u={0,θσx}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=\{0,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\}.

  4. (iv)

    wC2=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1, wσx=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1:
    As previously, we can set ρC2,u={0,nC2​π}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=\{0,n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}\pi\}. Equation (154) then implies ρσx,u={0,nσx​π}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=\{0,n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\pi\}.

B.1.2 Time-reversal symmetry

Having determined all solutions corresponding to the lattice space-group symmetries, we now turn to time-reversal symmetry. As a first step, we substitute the solution (118) into Eqs. (103) and (104), yielding:

Δ1​ϕ𝒯=θ𝒯​T1+y​θ​[1−(−1)w𝒯]\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{1}}+y\theta[1-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}}] (156)
Δ2​ϕ𝒯​(x,y,u)=θ𝒯​T2.\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y,u)=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{2}}\,. (157)

The consistency relations for time-reversal symmetry, analogous to Eqs. (121) and (125), are

Δ1​ϕ𝒯​(x,y,u)+Δ2​ϕ𝒯​(x−1,y,u)\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y,u)+\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x-1,y,u)
=Δ2​ϕ𝒯​(x,y,u)+Δ1​ϕ𝒯​(x,y−1,u)\displaystyle=\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y,u)+\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y-1,u) (158)

which impose the following constraint:

B.2 U(1) class with wT1=0,wT2=1w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}=0,\,w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}=1

B.2.1 Lattice symmetries

In this class of U(1) PSGs, the translation gauge transformations take the general form

WT1​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u) =ℱz​(ϕT1​(x,y,u)),\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u)), (193)
WT2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u) =ℱz​(ϕT2​(x,y,u))​(ι˙​τ1).\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{z}(\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u))(\dot{\iota}\tau^{1})\,. (194)

Analogous to the case with wT1=wT2=0w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}=w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}=0, one can perform a local gauge transformation such that

ϕT2​(x,y,u)=ϕT1​(x,0,u)=0.\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u)=\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,0,u)=0\,. (195)

To determine ϕT1​(x,y,u)\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u), we use Eq. (92) together with the above gauge choice, which yields

ϕT1​(x,y,u)=12​(1−(−1)y+1)​θ.\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u)=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(1-(-1)^{y+1}\bigr)\theta\,. (196)

After a global phase shift and redefining θ→2​θ\theta\rightarrow 2\theta, the resulting projective translations are

WT2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u) =ι˙​τx.\displaystyle=\dot{\iota}\tau^{x}\,. (198)

Substituting Eqs. (197) and (198) into Eqs. (93) and (94), respectively, we obtain

Δ1​ϕC2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{1}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) =−(−1)wC2​θC2​T1+(−1)y​θ​[1+(−1)wC2],\displaystyle=-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}+(-1)^{y}\theta\bigl[1+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}}\bigr],
Δ2​ϕC2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle\Delta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2}\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) =(−1)wC2−y​θC2​T2,\displaystyle=(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}-y}\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}\,, (199)

which must satisfy the consistency relation (121). This leads to the following constraint on θ\theta:

Using this constraint, the solution for ϕC2\phi^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}} follows from Eq. (199):

where ζy=12​(1+(−1)y)\zeta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{y}=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(1+(-1)^{y}\bigr).

A similar analysis can be applied to σx\sigma^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{x} using Eqs. (95) and (96), together with the consistency condition (125), which imposes

−(−1)wσx​y​θ+ρσx,u.\displaystyle-(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}y\theta+\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}\,. (203)

+(−1)wσx​ρσx,u¯\displaystyle+(-1)^{w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}}\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}} =θC2​σx,\displaystyle=\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}},

We now analyze the PSG solutions associated with time-reversal symmetry. From Eqs. (103) and (104), we arrive at

w𝒯w_{\mathcal{T}} == 00: Equation (102) requires θ𝒯​Ti=n𝒯​Ti​π\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{i}}=n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{i}}\pi. Furthermore, solving Eqs. (105) and (106) gives θ𝒯​T1=0\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}T_{1}}=0, with

wC2=1,wσx=1:\displaystyle w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}=1,\;w^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=1: ρ𝒯,u={0,θ𝒯},\displaystyle\quad\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T},u}=\{0,\theta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}\}, (225)
All other cases:\displaystyle\text{All other cases}: ρ𝒯,u={0,n𝒯​π}.\displaystyle\quad\rho^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T},u}=\{0,n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathcal{T}}\pi\}\,. (226)

Appendix C ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} projective symmetry groups

In this section, we derive the algebraic solutions for projective symmetry groups assuming a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} invariant gauge group. The Ansatz now incorporates both hopping and pairing terms, leading to the general form

ui​j=ι˙​χi​j0​τ0+χi​j3​τ3+Δi​j1​τ1+Δi​j2​τ2.u^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{ij}=\dot{\iota}\chi^{0}_{ij}\tau^{0}+\chi_{ij}^{3}\tau^{3}+\Delta_{ij}^{1}\tau^{1}+\Delta_{ij}^{2}\tau^{2}. (227)

Here, the coefficients of τ3\tau^{3} and τ0\tau^{0} correspond to real and imaginary hopping amplitudes, respectively, while the coefficients of τ1\tau^{1} and τ2\tau^{2} correspond to real and imaginary pairing amplitudes. The elements of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} IGG are parameterized by η…∈{±1}\eta_{\ldots}\in\{\pm 1\}. We derive the projective realizations of the lattice and time-reversal symmetries separately in the following subsections.

C.1 Lattice symmetries

Analogous to the U(1) case, an appropriate choice of local gauge allows one to set WT1​(x,0,u)=WT2​(x,y,u)=τ0W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,0,u)=W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u)=\tau^{0}. Substituting this into the gauge condition (92) yields the projective representations of the translations:

WT1​(x,y,u)=ηT1y​τ0,WT2​(x,y,u)=τ0.W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{T_{1}}^{y}\tau^{0},\quad W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u)=\tau^{0}\,. (228)

To determine the PSG for C2C_{2}, we insert Eq. (228) into Eqs. (93) and (94), leading to the recursion relations

WC2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) =ηC2​T1​WC2​(x−1,y,u),\displaystyle=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x-1,y,u), (229)
WC2​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) =ηC2​T2​WC2​(x,y−1,u),\displaystyle=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{2}}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y-1,u),\, (230)

solving which gives

WC2​(x,y,u)=ηC2​T2y​ηC2​T1x​WC2​(0,0,u).W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{C_{2}T_{2}}^{y}\eta_{C_{2}T_{1}}^{x}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(0,0,u)\,. (231)

Similarly, using Eqs. (95), (96) and (228), we obtain

Wσx​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) =ησx​T1​Wσx​(x−1,y,u),\displaystyle=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x-1,y,u), (232)
Wσx​(x,y,u)\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) =ηT1−y+1​ησx​T2​Wσx​(x,y−1,u),\displaystyle=\eta_{T_{1}}^{-y+1}\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y-1,u), (233)

which are solved by

Wσx​(x,y,u)=ηT1−y⁡(y−1)2​ησx​T2y​ησx​T1x​Wσx​(0,0,u).\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{T_{1}}^{-\frac{y(y-1)}{2}}\eta_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}^{y}\eta_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}^{x}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(0,0,u)\,. (234)

From Eq. (97), we obtain

WC2,u​Wσx,u¯​WC2,u​Wσx,u¯\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}} =ηC2​σx​τ0,\displaystyle=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}, (235)
ηC2​T1\displaystyle\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}T_{1}} =ησx​T1.\displaystyle=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}. (236)

Similarly, Eq. (98) yields

WC2,u​WC2,u¯=ηC2​τ0,\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},\bar{u}}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}\tau^{0}, (237)

while Eq. (99) gives

Wσx,u​Wσx,u¯\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}} =ησx​τ0,\displaystyle=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}, (238)
ησx​T1\displaystyle\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}} =ηT1.\displaystyle=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}. (239)

Further gauge fixing can be implemented through a transformation of the form

W⁡(x,y,u)=ηxx​ηyy​τ0,\displaystyle W(x,y,u)=\eta_{x}^{x}\eta_{y}^{y}\tau^{0}, (240)

which leaves the translational gauge structure unchanged, up to global sign factors. These global signs can be absorbed into the IGG freedom, allowing us to set one of them to +1+1 without loss of generality. Under this transformation, the operators WC2​(x,y,u){W}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u) and Wσx​(x,y,u){W}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u) transform as

W~C2​(x,y,u)=ηC2​T2y​ηC2​T1x​WC2,u,\displaystyle\tilde{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{C_{2}T_{2}}^{y}\eta_{C_{2}T_{1}}^{x}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (241)
W~σx​(x,y,u)=ηxy​ηT1−y⁡(y−1)2​ησx​T2y​ησx​T1x​Wσx,u.\displaystyle\tilde{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{x}^{y}\eta_{T_{1}}^{-\frac{y(y-1)}{2}}\eta_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}^{y}\eta_{\sigma_{x}T_{1}}^{x}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}. (242)

By choosing ηx=ησx​T2\eta_{x}=\eta_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}}, one can eliminate the parameter ησx​T2\eta_{\sigma_{x}T_{2}} from WσxW_{\sigma_{x}}. In this gauge, the solutions take the form

WT1​(x,y,u)=ηT1y​τ0,WT2​(x,y,u)=τ0,\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{1}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{T_{1}}^{y}\tau^{0},\quad W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{T_{2}}(x,y,u)=\tau^{0}, (243)
WC2​(x,y,u)=ηC2​T2y​ηT1x​WC2,u,\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{C_{2}T_{2}}^{y}\eta_{T_{1}}^{x}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}, (244)
Wσx​(x,y,u)=ηT1−y⁡(y−1)2+x​Wσx,u.\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}(x,y,u)=\eta_{T_{1}}^{-\frac{y(y-1)}{2}+x}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}. (245)

For notational convenience, we omit the tilde in what follows.

Next, combining (97)–(99), we obtain the constraints

WC2,u​WC2,u¯=ηC2​τ0,\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},\bar{u}}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}}\tau^{0}, (246)
Wσx,u​Wσx,u¯=ησx​τ0,\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}, (247)
WC2,u​Wσx,u¯​WC2,u​Wσx,u¯=ηC2​σx​τ0.\displaystyle W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},\bar{u}}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}. (248)

At this stage, one may still perform a sublattice-dependent gauge transformation of the form W⁡(x,y,u)=WuW(x,y,u)=W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{u}, under which the sublattice-dependent components transform as

W~σx,u=Wu†​Wσx,u​Wu¯.\displaystyle\tilde{W}^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}=W^{\dagger}_{u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x},u}W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\bar{u}}. (250)

Wσx={τ0,ησx​τ0}.W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}=\{\tau^{0},\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}\}. (251)

Combining Eq. (246) with Eq. (251), we find

WC2,u2=ηC2​σx​τ0⇒WC2,12=WC2,22=ηC2​σx​τ0,\displaystyle W_{C_{2},u}^{2}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}\;\;\Rightarrow\;\;W_{C_{2},1}^{2}=W_{C_{2},2}^{2}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}\tau^{0}, (252)

leading to two distinct cases:

ηC2​σx=+1\displaystyle\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}=+1 :WC2,u=ηC,u​τ0,\displaystyle:W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C,u}\tau^{0}, (253)
ηC2​σx=−1\displaystyle\eta^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2}\sigma_{x}}=-1 :WC2,u=i​α→C2,u⋅τ→.\displaystyle:W^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{C_{2},u}=i\vec{\alpha}_{C_{2},u}\cdot\vec{\tau}. (254)
